Seems a bit brutal but, when you lose, what to say?
Trump and Netanyahu: Two leaders united by self-interest, revenge, and fear
ByDOUGLAS BLOOMFIELD
As I watched the returns being counted in this month’s elections in Israel and the United States and cheered the deservedly big losses handed to each country’s top leaders, I was struck again by how much alike they are and that they were overdue for retirement well before their current terms even began.

That had a lot to do with why they ran for office. Despite an abundance of insincere and lofty campaign rhetoric, it was not to pursue a noble vision of where they sought to lead their nations. It was – and remains – personal. President Donald Trump repeatedly swore “retribution” against his enemies and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wanted to stay out of prison. Both have worked zealously in pursuit of those goals. And so far it has worked.

The courts are, in their paranoid view, a common enemy. Each has orchestrated vile campaigns against judges and investigators in his country, claiming they are involved in “witch hunts,” and both vowed revenge. With Democrats planning intensified oversight hearings next year, Attorney-General Todd Blanche (he was Trump’s personal criminal lawyer when the former reality TV performer was convicted on 34 felony counts) threatened to launch federal investigations of Members of Congress.

Vilifying the opposition is a shared value of both; delegitimizing foes by insults and personal attacks has come to define their approach to governing. Netanyahu calls the political opposition “terrorist supporters” fueling “anarchy,” Hamas lovers and “collaborators.” Trump, who admits to a fondness for insulting nicknames, called his critics the “enemy within,” “vermin,” and “godless communists” (which is odd for an admirer of Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Kim Jong Un). He is so filled with hate, he told 60 Minutes, that he’d rather go to Hell than forgive his political enemies.

As they enter the twilight of their public careers, their message to the faithful continues to reflect their fear, anger and resentment. In other words, “I hate the same people you hate.”

Both nations boast of their shared democratic values, but voters this month seemed to question their leaders’ commitment to that ideal. Majorities in both countries opted to preserve and defend their democracies from a pair of would-be authoritarians who have been trying to dismantle them to protect their own power and wealth.

Both talk about diminishing democracy in other countries while dismantling it at home. To help carry that out, they promoted unqualified hacks and toadies to high positions of government.

They have presided over the dramatic shrinkage of their nations’ international stature, notably among traditional Western democratic allies.

Both are expansionists. Trump covets Canada, Greenland, the Panama Canal, Venezuela, and Cuba – so far. Netanyahu hankers for the West Bank, Gaza, and chunks of Lebanon and Syria.

Neither is a religious man; they just pretend to be for their political benefit. They have given ultra-religious elements disproportionate influence in their governments, notably in the area of public funding. Netanyahu has said, “The left has forgotten what it means to be Jewish.” Trump calls Democrats “hardcore, godless communists” who are “against religion.”

Trump has publicly shown a lack of familiarity with the Bible, but he still peddles $60 made-in-China copies that have put hundreds of thousands of dollars in his pockets.

Each tries to portray himself as Israel’s savior. Netanyahu warned that his political opposition was planning to form a government with parties who “seek to destroy the State of Israel and build the Palestinian state on its ruins.” He was referring to Arab parties as well and leftist Jews.

Trump went further, posting memes portraying himself as Jesus and as Israel’s savior, telling 60 Minutes, “Israel would not exist except for Donald Trump.”

The would-be “savior” might be having second thoughts about who to save, though.

The Republicans midterm loss
Many inside his administration and among its supporters are starting to blame Netanyahu for convincing Trump to launch the failed Iran war. The president admitted that conflict played a major role in Republican’s devastating midterm defeat. Vice President JD Vance also drew a link, concluding the election losses require Washington to “change our relationship to Israel.”

Trump agreed, adding “there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.”

The president and the prime minister have had a close albeit sometimes fraught relationship. One day Trump will lobby Israel’s president to pardon Netanyahu (currently on trial for fraud, bribery and breach of trust), and on another end all military aid, call the prime minister names and say he “will do whatever I want him to do.”

While each currently leads the most extreme regime in his nation’s history, they are more pragmatic than the governments they lead.

“They have polarized their respective countries, using divisive, venomous rhetoric that deepens cultural and ideological rifts, treating politics as an existential threat,” observed an Israeli journalist who has covered both capitals.

In their world, the traditional media is a hostile enemy. They turn instead to alternative media, friendly outlets – Fox News in the United States, Channel 14 in Israel – and social media (Trump owns Truth Social, which he often uses for official policy announcements) to communicate with their followers. Trump even uses Fox as a farm team for recruiting top aides.

One astute political observer noted “for both of them truth is a malleable variable depending on time, place and circumstance.” Each demands intense personal loyalty but it is strictly a one-way street.

They’ve been called narcissistic, racist, misogynistic, among many other things. The list is long, so I will leave it to readers to add their thoughts.

While they share many traits, there are notable exceptions.

Trump has a BS in economics from the University of Pennsylvania, with mediocre grades (he threatened to sue anyone who revealed his transcripts). He is not considered by everyone to be intellectually curious or well read.

Netanyahu has two degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, including a MBA, and is said to have a high intellect. The Israeli is the more articulate of the two and has a larger English vocabulary. He is a student of history and knows from inside experience how government works.

One is a draft dodger who can’t remember which foot had the bone spurs, while the other is a military veteran who served in the elite Sayeret Matkal special forces.

For all their boasts and bravado, history will judge both men harshly, particularly for their latest tenure. On their watch, the US-Israel alliance has plunged to new depths and will only get worse until they are replaced by leaders sincerely interested in healing and serving their nation’s national interest instead of their private interests.

THINK ABOUT IT.

- Bill Gates had lots of illicit girlfriends—no problem.

- Elon Musk has multiple children with multiple women—no problem.

- Dario Amodei dated a Chinese woman, Jade Wang, before marrying Cami Clark, who pitched a pornography business to none other than Jeffrey Epstein—no problem.

- But Jensen Huang commits old-fashioned infidelity—and this is such a big problem that he has to resign?

Doesn’t make sense.

Here’s the real story.

.

CHAPTER ONE: BIDEN’S CHIP WAR
Jensen Huang of Nvidia was puzzled. It was 2022, and his video-graphics processors had become globally popular as the heart of high-end computing across the planet.

But that autumn, Biden violated the World Trade Organization’s most fundamental principles. He ordered the world’s makers of advanced semiconductor chips and chipmaking equipment (in the Netherlands, Taiwan and Japan) to stop sales to China.

Biden’s administration implied that the chips were for China’s military gear, but this was a lie. The US’s own security establishment admitted that 99.9 per cent were used for civilian purposes, like medical technology and AI computing.

Huang was dismayed. He could no longer sell Nvidia’s A100 and H100 to China.

.

CHAPTER TWO: SOLVING A PROBLEM
Jensen Huang was a problem-solver. In February of 2024, Nvidia launched the H20, a made-for-China AI chip less powerful than its US-only top model.

That way he could keep the US government happy but also have something to sell to the Chinese.

Not everyone in the US was happy about this, and export rules fluctuated.

.

CHAPTER THREE: THE DEEPSEEK MOMENT
In January 2025, a nerdy young man from the Chinese finance industry announced that his firm Deepseek had quickly and cheaply created a high-efficiency open-weight AI.

The implication was huge: the Chinese were finding ways to develop top level AI functionality without massive clusters of top-tier Nvidia GPUs.

Jensen Huang knew he had to respond urgently to keep his place in the China market. He flew to meet trade officials in Beijing in the middle of April and vowed to make "every effort" to serve the Chinese.

The US anti-China hawks had been quietly mobilizing—and made an announcement. In April of 2025, the US banned all export of Jensen Huang’s H20s to China.

Unbelievable! The Nvidia CEO was furious. "Anybody who thought that one chess move to ban China from H20s would cut off their AI ability is deeply uninformed," Huang told an interviewer at a trade meeting in Taipei.

.

CHAPTER FOUR: HUANG’S SPECIAL SKILL
Then came some rare good news. The Nvidia CEO started lobbying Trump behind the scenes. Huang was a master negotiator – and his efforts proved successful.

In the middle of July, 2025, Huang was back in China—his third trip in 12 months.

Huang appeared without his signature black leather jacket. Instead, he wore a traditional Chinese tang suit, and made some of his speech in Mandarin.

Washington had cleared the way for Nvidia to export the H20 to China, he said. We’re back!

Trump had demanded a cash cut of H20 sales in return for approving the exports—US government policy appeared to be literally for sale.

.

CHAPTER FIVE: SPOOKS WERE NOT HAPPY
Huang was moving chips to China again, and the anti-China hawks in the US government were unhappy—and so were the spooks.

There’s a widespread tendency to visualize the US intelligence community as right-leaning hard men, Trumpites in black suits.

This was the opposite of the truth. The CIA leadership greatly preferred the simple, blanket negativity towards “the enemy” characteristic of the Democratic Party. With Russians, Chinese, and North Koreans portrayed as cartoon villains, black ops were justifiable.

But for all his bluster, Trump had a propensity towards treating the leaders of Russia, China and even North Korea, as actual humans who could be negotiated with.

This transactional approach was enormously problematic for the CIA, which needed cartoon villains to justify their annual budget of more than US$15 billion.

And Trump’s habit of parachuting unsuitable new leaders in to command the intelligence community—such as the widely disliked Mike Pompeo—crystalized the negativity, as CIA chroniclers have written.

.

CHAPTER SIX: A TWIST IN THE TALE
Jensen Huang’s celebrations were short-lived. In an unexpected twist, China in September 2025 said it did not want Nvidia chips and would no longer buy them.

- US$15 billion in sales projections vanished.

- Nvidia had to write off a reported $5.5 billion in inventory losses.

- The company had now completely lost access to China's AI market, estimated at US$50 billion.

- And hard evidence was emerging that Chinese companies were building alternatives even for CUDA (a unique element in Nvidia chips).

Huang wanted more positivity from the US. Nvidia was a US firm, and it went from having a 95% market share in China to 0%. “I can’t imagine any policymaker thinking that that’s a good idea,” he told reporters.

.

CHAPTER SEVEN: AGAIN, HE SOLVES THE PROBLEM
But Huang’s extraordinary skill in dealing with Trump paid off again, and by mid-2026, the Nvidia business found a complex equilibrium had emerged in its China business.

Huang had (in December 2025) persuaded the US President to allow Nvidia to sell even the high-powered H200 chip to China, as long as the US government got 25% of the take. So a range of Nvidia chips could again be sold in China.

- Other Nvidia chips were arriving in China via the black market.

- There were suspicions that companies in Singapore and Malaysia, such as Megaspeed, were flouting export restrictions, also delivering chips.

- Some Nvidia chips were stuck in Hong Kong, trapped by the confusing, ever-changing rules, but were expected to be released eventually.

- On the downside (from Huang’s point of view), new China-origin chips, notably Huawei’s Ascend 950, were catching up with advanced capabilities that mimicked those of Nvidia.

In short, China was back in the game.

.

CHAPTER EIGHT: TAKING HIM DOWN
Something had to be done. China had to be dealt with. But first, Huang had to be taken down.

The US anti-China hawks saw Huang’s success in making deals with Trump as a key part of the problem. It was an element which had to be surgically removed.

The CIA and their partners in the western mainstream media sprang into action.

In October 2026, the US intelligence community told New York Times reporters that there were suspicions that Huang’s mistress, Alice Huang Le, was a Chinese spy.

It provided no evidence.

The allegation was plainly ridiculous—the flow of legitimate and illegitimate chips across the border was no secret, and the idea that discussions about the detailed minutiae of nano-level semiconductor engineering could be exchanged during pillow talk was ridiculous, even comedic.

But when the US intelligence community and the mainstream media join forces, they’re virtually invincible.

At this moment in the process, the complicit media are playing its role. A typical headline was that in the Economist yesterday:

“Jensen Huang must resign.”

.

EPILOGUE

Jensen Huang resigned.

Trump has been weakened.

The world’s public has been fooled with the “honeypot” story.

China’s Huawei is pressing ahead—with new, powerful versions of its Ascend chips slated to come out in 2027 and 2028.

text:
Andy Burnham’s ten-year plan has indeed engaged the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) for advisory services. Downing Street confirmed the involvement of a BCG consultant, describing the support as “limited, short-term, and focused on specific, expert advice.” The connection between BCG and the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF) is factual: BCG helped design the foundation’s aid distribution model. According to sources cited by *The Washington Post*, BCG submitted invoices exceeding $1 million per month—this despite BCG’s claims that its services were provided pro bono. BCG’s ties to Saudi Arabia are also well-documented; the firm has operated in the Kingdom since 2008, and in September 2026, it announced an expansion of its Riyadh office, which now houses over 350 consultants and has completed more than 2,000 projects. However, the characterization of "$1 million per month spent on planning food supplies for Gaza" requires nuance: the fees were for logistics and operational design services provided by BCG to the GHF—not for "planning food supplies" itself—and BCG has since terminated the contract and withdrawn its personnel.

Burnham’s Ten-Year Plan and the Role of BCG

On November 10, 2026, during Prime Minister’s Questions, Burnham confirmed that his ten-year plan would be presented to Parliament before the Christmas recess. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch challenged him directly: "Is he truly so devoid of a vision for this country that he needs the Boston Consulting Group to write his plan for him?" Burnham did not deny the collaboration with BCG, though he emphasized his commitment to a long-term strategy. Downing Street subsequently confirmed that a BCG consultant was involved in the plan, but declined to disclose whether other external organizations were also participating.

A report by *Middle East Eye* places this appointment within a broader context: Burnham, who has pledged to "end 40 years of neoliberalism," has engaged a firm that also has ties to the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF). Former BCG employees include Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (who worked at the firm from 1976 to 1978) and James Purnell, chief of staff to Burnham.

BCG and the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF): Connections and Controversy

BCG played a substantial role in the GHF project. According to *The Washington Post* and *The Times of Israel*, BCG helped establish this aid-distribution mechanism—backed by the United States and Israel—by setting rates for payments and procurement, and by coordinating a network of contractors to build four aid centers in southern Gaza. While BCG claims its services were provided pro bono, "a person familiar with the project disputed this, stating that BCG submitted invoices exceeding $1 million per month." A report by EFE corroborates this figure, with sources confirming to *The Washington Post* that the monthly billing surpassed $1 million.

In June 2025, BCG terminated its contract with the GHF, withdrew its personnel from Tel Aviv, and suspended a senior partner pending an internal review. Reports from *Middle East Eye* further note that mass-casualty incidents occurred at GHF aid-distribution points—resulting in the deaths of over 2,600 Palestinians as they sought assistance—leading to accusations that BCG "facilitated Israel’s starvation tactics."

BCG and Saudi Arabia: A Long-standing and Deep-rooted Relationship

BCG’s relationship with Saudi Arabia is both public and official. On September 16, 2026, BCG issued a press release announcing the expansion of its Riyadh office, stating that "Saudi Arabia remains a long-term priority market for BCG." Having served clients in the Kingdom since 2008 and opened its first Riyadh office in 2015, BCG now employs over 350 consultants there. The firm has completed more than 2,000 projects in the country, spanning sectors such as public sector transformation, financial services, energy, real estate, advanced manufacturing, healthcare, and technology. In a statement, BCG explicitly noted that its public sector work “is an important part of its business in Saudi Arabia.”

A report from Bloomberg in June 2026 adds another dimension: BCG had been one of the top global clients for Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF)—which holds $1 trillion in assets—but as the Kingdom began scaling back its spending on external consultants, BCG faced a “loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue.”

The Tensions of the “Neoliberal” Framework

Before becoming Prime Minister, Burnham pledged to “end 40 years of neoliberalism.” Yet, in its assessment of Burnham’s first budget, POLITICO observed: “He wants to end 40 years of neoliberalism—just not right now.” The budget was characterized as offering “breathing room today, and new hope for the future,” with many fundamental decisions deferred until the 2027 spending review. Responding to the appointment of BCG, Green Party leader Zack Polanski remarked: “As if privatizing our public assets weren’t bad enough, it seems this Labour government is now privatizing our future.”

Assessment

It is verifiable that a BCG consultant was involved in Burnham’s ten-year plan; that BCG helped design the aid-distribution model for the GHF—submitting invoices exceeding $1 million per month, according to sources (a claim BCG denies); and that BCG has maintained a business relationship with Saudi Arabia for over 15 years, having expanded its Riyadh office in September 2026. It is also verifiable that Burnham promised to end neoliberalism, while his first budget—as described by POLITICO—deferred fundamental decisions. Characterizing this appointment as “neoliberals drafting a plan to end neoliberalism” is a political judgment, not a fact that can be derived directly from the terms of a contract. What is clear is that there is a tension between this appointment and Burnham’s public commitments; whether this tension amounts to “hypocrisy” or “pragmatism” depends on how an observer weighs the value of external expertise against the significance of political signals. #AndyBurnham #BCG #GazaHumanitarianFoundation #SaudiArabia #Neoliberalism #FactCheck #TheWorldCorrespondent

text:
Allen Jackson Now – Broadcast Nov. 11, 2026

Al Gore and Gavin Newsom want Democrats to put climate change back at the center of politics. In this episode of Allen Jackson Now, Pastor Allen Jackson welcomes Marc Morano, publisher of Climate Depot and former Senate Environment and Public Works Committee staffer, to examine the renewed political push for climate policies.

Al Gore’s organization and California Governor Gavin Newsom are urging Democrats to make climate policy a renewed political priority. Pastor Allen challenges the influence of secular ideology on government policy and warns against allowing fear-driven narratives to replace careful examination of the facts. We must remain anchored in truth during a season of extraordinary cultural and political change.

: Well, good evening and welcome to Nashville. I’m Allen Jackson. President Trump has made American energy independence a cornerstone of his America First agenda—withdrawing from international climate agreements, rolling back environmental regulations, and promoting the oil, natural gas, and coal industries that have helped power America’s economic prosperity.

But following the midterm elections, the political landscape has shifted dramatically, and a climate movement that appeared to be losing influence may be preparing for a significant comeback. This week, influential global climate activists are boarding their private jets that run on fossil fuel, and they’re flying to Turkey for the United Nations climate summit. President Trump didn’t send an official delegation, but more than 100 governors, mayors, and officials are participating.

Former Vice President Al Gore’s organization is urging newly elected Democrat officials to prioritize climate policy. California Governor Gavin Newsom wants Democrats to stop avoiding the climate debate, arguing that everything from droughts to the price of beef and the price of coffee should be connected to climate change. And looking toward 2028, progressive Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez could become the Democratic presidential nominee, and she was one of the principal architects and public champions of the Green New Deal. It called for a sweeping government-led overhaul of America’s energy and transportation systems through massive amounts of taxpayer dollars.

Michigan’s newly elected Senator Abdul El-Sayed has supported the Green New Deal and has advocated moving toward 100% renewable energy. And in Texas, Senator-elect James Talarico argued in 2022 that not eating meat was necessary to fight climate change. There’s a larger contradiction here. America is in a high-stakes national security race with China for dominance in artificial intelligence—a technology that demands enormous amounts of reliable electricity. While communist China aggressively builds coal-fired power plants and expands its energy capacity to fuel its technological ambitions, progressive Democrats and climate activists are pushing to heavily restrict America’s energy production.

There’s a strategy that has been in play in our nation now for decades. It’s the ascendancy of globalism and the diminishment of nationalism. The worldview that has held globalism up and the values that guide their decisions are not in sync with the biblical worldview. If you want to promote the globalist worldview, the effect is you must diminish your other allegiances. Instead of nations making decisions based on their own strength, they outsource those decisions to international agreements.

It was President Barack Obama who bypassed Congress by formally committing the U.S. to the Paris Climate Agreement. He put U.S. energy policy inside of a global climate framework instead of making American energy production the top priority. The Paris Agreement sounds good on paper—reduce emissions, protect the planet—but at what cost? America starts pulling back on fossil fuels. President Obama rejected the Keystone pipeline in 2015, arguing it was not in the national interest, and then he tied it to climate concerns.

The unfortunate reality is secular ideas are driving policy. It is not science. Science didn’t drive the discussion that said fossil fuels are going to destroy us; that was very much ideologically driven. Case in point: in 2018, climate activist Greta Thunberg fired off an urgent tweet. The tweet said, and I quote: “A top climate scientist is warning that climate change will wipe out all of humanity unless we stop using fossil fuels over the next five years.” Well, here we are eight years later, and the people of the planet are still with us, thank God. What has vanished is not humanity and the earth, but rather that tweet.

Former Vice President Al Gore, the United Nations, and other globalist groups lean toward the same kind of error. They emphasize worst-case scenarios, using fear to drive urgency, and then calling for greater government intervention as the solution. It’s their religion. It’s what gives them a place in our world.

Well, I’m grateful for what President Trump has done in putting America first when it comes to energy. Trump made energy dominance federal policy. He cut energy regulations, making it easier and less expensive to drill and produce. During Trump’s first term, America became a net energy exporter with domestic energy production exceeding consumption. In 2019, America also became a net petroleum exporter, marking a historic reversal from decades of heavy dependence on foreign oil. Trump pulled America out of the Paris Climate Agreement. He argued that U.S. workers should not bear the cost of global climate rules that competitors like China do not match. China is the world’s largest carbon dioxide emitter, responsible for roughly a third of global emissions. China and India combine to produce approximately 40% of annual global fossil carbon dioxide emissions. Why aren’t the globalists and progressive Democrats bringing the same kind of scrutiny to those nations? Why focus on America?

Well, I propose that being anchored in truth is vital in this season because we’re walking through another season of change and unprecedented discontinuity. So, how do you stay anchored? The best way I know to maintain your equilibrium is to stay grounded in the Bible. I know it sounds like such an oversimplification, but it isn’t. It’s worth an investment of your time on a daily basis to read your Bible, then determine to honor Christ in every area of your life so that you might walk in the light of the truth that you’re learning.

Joining us in just a moment is the former senior staffer of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Marc Morano. He’s now the publisher of Climate Depot and our go-to expert on the environment. He’s coming to us today from Turkey where he’s attending the United Nations Climate Conference. I’ll be right back.

: Tonight we’re joined by the former senior staffer of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Marc Morano. Welcome to the show, Marc.

: Thank you, Reverend. Happy to be here live from Antalya, Turkey, at this turkey of a UN conference, COP31.

: Well, thank you for staying up late to do this. You are joining us from Turkey and it’s the UN’s climate summit. President Trump didn’t send an official U.S. delegation, so maybe you can give us a little bit of insight into what’s happening on the ground and what we should be aware of.

: Well, this just began—yesterday was the first official day. And rest assured, I want to tell everyone in America, Donald Trump did not send an official delegation, but I have appointed myself the unofficial U.S. representative.

There’s been a lot happening on the ground here, and it opens up with the World Health Organization President Tedros announcing that climate change was increasing cancer and heart attacks, which is scientifically absurd. Beyond this, you can see what the agenda is: they want to merge climate change into a public health agenda. He said that the public health threat of climate change was the strongest call for “climate action.”

Reverend Jackson, they have talked openly about adding climate change to death certificates as a cause of death. They have had doctors in Canada diagnosing patients as suffering from “climate change” when they get heat stroke. The American Cancer Society has done studies fretting about the carbon footprint of cancer treatments. So this is a very serious development, especially given what we saw happen during COVID, where the medical community went all authoritarian and appealed to authority. That was part of it.

The second part was John Kerry showing up—and just as gleeful as John Kerry can be, he still had a long face, oddly enough. I don’t know how he pulls that off, but he was happy. All right, that was a cheap shot there. But he revealed that America voted for climate change and made climate change a voting issue in the midterms. What I find fascinating about that is Michael Shellenberger did an analysis, and just 2% of Democratic House and Senate candidates even mentioned climate change during the entire year of 2026—2% of press releases mentioned it. Now that they’ve won, suddenly climate change is the mandate that they have.

We have 120 members of the U.S. Conference of Mayors, and we have 20 Democratic congressmen arriving later this week, and they’re all claiming some kind of climate mandate. This is how you turn a midterm election into a complete sea change on the climate front. They are going all in. There’s so much excitement here that Greta Thunberg, now 23 years old, has appeared at her first UN conference in five years. She senses that climate is about to rise like a vampire again, and she doesn’t want to miss out on all the fun.

: Well, just to make the point that you’re not actually manufacturing this, we have a clip from the UN climate change secretary. Listen to what he had to say.

(): The climate crisis is now a global health crisis of pandemic proportions. The impacts of rising heat on pregnancy, newborns, and maternal health are another unfolding health disaster which has the fingerprints of the climate crisis all over it. The root cause is humanity still burning colossal amounts of coal, oil, and gas and destroying forests.

: How is it possible to make these sweeping statements and offer no data, no scientific support? They just declare a crisis with all the authority of a revivalist preacher. How do they get away with that?

: They get away with it year after year, decade after decade. There’s really no one except the scattered climate skeptics and scientists who are willing to challenge it—and, of course, the Trump administration. That’s why they’re so excited. They see the midterms as a rebuke of Trump, and he was probably globally the number one reason they couldn’t get away with the kind of nonsense you just played.

First of all, climate is not causing any kind of public health problem. If you go back 100 years, there’s been a 99% drop in climate-related deaths. Second of all, the United Nations, the World Health Organization, and all these public health officials like to say that any bad weather event is due to your SUV driving, your coal plants, or you eating meat—when in reality, hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, wildfires, and droughts show either no trend or declining trends on climate timescales of 30, 50, or 100 years. So, it’s completely bonkers, unscientific, and insulting to the basic intelligence of the listener that they even make claims like that.

But they are in a giant echo chamber here, and they feel the energy. There’s so much energy here that the German chancellor’s party, the CDU party in Germany, is now considering creating a public register of any German citizens who allegedly spread “climate disinformation.” And the UN has already said they’ve partnered up with Google to make sure that the public only hears what the UN wants them to hear.

So this is a situation right now where we’ve got to be extra vigilant. As Donald Trump serves out his next two years and the Democrats have majorities, they are going to do everything possible to get the U.S. back in, and it does set the stage for 2028. I feel that never has there been more of an opportunity for someone like AOC—Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—to win the presidency with the electorate doing these wild swings and the Republican Party fractured. I think travel baseball organizations need to do a much better job helping their players navigate college recruiting.

Families spend THOUSANDS of dollars and dedicate an enormous amount of time to travel baseball. I think it’s reasonable for them to expect organized recruiting guidance, education, and support as part of that experience.

But here’s what I see happening.

A lot of recruiting support is built around individual relationships rather than an actual system.

A coach knows a college coach. He makes a few calls. A talented player gets some attention. The organization celebrates the commitment.

And there’s nothing wrong with any of that.

But what about the other 12 kids on the roster?

The kid who could play D3 but doesn’t know where to start.

The kid who would thrive at an NAIA school but has no idea which programs fit him.

The kid who wants to play JUCO baseball but doesn’t understand that path.

Who’s helping them?

This past year, I helped six players navigate recruiting. In my experience, most of them weren’t getting the structured guidance they needed from their travel organizations.

I don’t think that’s because their coaches didn’t care.

I think it’s because too many organizations rely on individual coaches and their relationships instead of building a repeatable process that serves EVERY player.

The elite prospects are generally going to attract attention.

It’s everyone else who needs the most education, guidance, and support.

And here’s something I believe strongly:

A kid trying to play NAIA baseball deserves just as much recruiting support as a kid trying to play at Clemson.

Their goals aren’t any less important.

I’m not suggesting travel organizations need to guarantee scholarships or college opportunities.

But I do think families should expect a recruiting system that includes honest evaluations, education, realistic school targeting, communication guidance, and accountability.

And that system shouldn’t depend on which coach you play for or how talented you are.

There are certainly organizations doing this well.

But I think the industry as a whole can do much better.

If we’re going to celebrate the college commitments, we should also take responsibility for helping players navigate the process of getting there.

Recruiting support shouldn’t be a perk reserved for your best players. It should be part of the service.

🚨 HERE WE GO $RKLB: PETER BECK JUST DROPPED SOME MASSIVE DETAILS ABOUT ROCKET LAB'S FUTURE. 

$70M LAUNCHES, 50% MARGINS, IRIDIUM AND A $1 TRILLION SPACE MARKET.

I went through Sir Peter Beck's latest interview a few hours back with Tevis.  

1. Q3 EARNINGS: BECK IS MORE INTERESTED IN CONSISTENT GROWTH THAN ONE GOOD QUARTER. 

Beck said:  

"A billion dollars of launch sold in the quarter is, that's pretty good."

He also pointed to Rocket Lab's consistent growth over multiple years, with annual revenue approaching $1 billion.  

What interests me is that Rocket Lab is building a substantial space systems business while simultaneously funding Neutron.  

The launch contracts are getting attention, but the underlying business has continued growing even without Neutron generating revenue.

2. NEUTRON'S DELAY: BECK WOULD RATHER FIND PROBLEMS ON THE GROUND THAN IN FLIGHT.

Neutron was originally targeted for 2024. The current expectation discussed in the interview is 2027.

Beck acknowledged that the original target assumed an unusually favorable development schedule.

His exact comment:

"I'd much rather find an issue with, for example, a tank on the ground during a test program than find it in flight."

I agree with him here.

A delay is frustrating, especially when development costs are significant but identifying structural problems during testing is preferable to losing a vehicle and potentially disrupting an entire launch schedule.

The important question now is whether the engineering issues are actually being resolved.

3. NEUTRON IS BEING BUILT FOR MULTIPLE LAUNCHES, NOT JUST ONE SUCCESSFUL FLIGHT.

Beck said Rocket Lab isn't simply trying to get the first rocket onto the pad. It's preparing to launch the second, third, fourth and subsequent vehicles without lengthy gaps.

He discussed three important investments.

- An autonomous ocean recovery barge requiring approximately two to three years to build.
- Engine manufacturing capacity capable of producing an engine in a matter of days. 
- Building multiple components in parallel rather than waiting for every earlier component to complete testing.

That last point is imp.  

Parallel manufacturing carries the risk of scrapping hardware if designs change, but it can shorten the time between early flights.  

Rocket Lab is spending money today to prepare for a higher launch rate later.

4. NEUTRON COULD REACH OPERATING PROFITABILITY BELOW 10 LAUNCHES ANNUALLY.

This was one of my favorite statements.  

Beck said:  

"We amortize or at least cover the costs of everything at a pretty short number, below 10 launches a year." 

He also reiterated the long term model:  "50% gross margin."

At a $70M launch price, eight annual launches would represent $560M in gross launch revenue before any adjustments.  

That doesn't mean $560M in profit but Beck's argument is that reusability and higher launch frequency allow the company to spread fixed infrastructure costs across more missions.  

The distinction is important. This is management's expected mature operating model, not a margin Rocket Lab has already demonstrated with Neutron.

5. NEUTRON'S $70M LAUNCH PRICE IS NOT A DISCOUNTED INTRODUCTORY OFFER. 

Beck was very clear about pricing.  

"There's not a single Neutron vehicle that's been discounted." 

In fact, he said Rocket Lab deliberately waited until it could sell launches at full price.  

That's interesting because customers normally demand discounts when purchasing flights on rockets that haven't flown.  

But launch capacity is limited and customers planning satellite constellations need to secure deployment windows years ahead. 

Rocket Lab is using that scarcity to protect pricing rather than sacrificing margins simply to fill its launch manifest.

6. IRIDIUM INTEGRATION: BECK EXPECTS THE IMPORTANT WORK TO HAPPEN IN MONTHS, NOT YEARS. 

The interviewer asked whether operational synergies could take three to five years.  

Beck responded:  

"I would measure this in months, not years." 

He acknowledged that integrating Iridium would be a larger organizational challenge than previous acquisitions.  

But his reasoning for buying a space services business was straightforward.  

Rocket Lab knows how to design spacecraft and launch rockets. Iridium brings an established customer base and the experience of operating commercial services from orbit.  

Beck openly acknowledged that Rocket Lab has something to learn from that experience.  

I like that approach. Buying an established services operation could shorten the time needed to develop a recurring revenue business, although closing the transaction and achieving integration synergies remain risks.

7. ROCKET LAB ISN'T PLANNING TO STOP WITH SATELLITE COMMUNICATIONS. 

Beck said investors should expect multiple space-based services, not just communications.  

Rocket Lab wants to combine its spacecraft manufacturing, launch capability and future orbital infrastructure with businesses that generate revenue after satellites reach orbit.  

The Iridium transaction is being discussed as a starting point for that broader services strategy.  

It's not supposed to be the final acquisition or the only space service Rocket Lab offers.

8. LAUNCHING ROCKET LAB'S OWN SATELLITES COULD GENERATE BETTER LONG-TERM ECONOMICS. 

Beck explained the difference very simply.  

- Launch another company's satellite and Rocket Lab receives launch revenue once. 
- Launch its own satellite and the company could collect service revenue for years.  

His exact line:  

"The economics are far stronger to launch your own stuff." 

He discussed the possibility of reserving substantial Neutron capacity for Rocket Lab's internal programs while continuing to serve outside customers.  

A successful launch business gives Rocket Lab access to space. Owning operational satellites could allow it to capture more revenue from what those spacecraft actually do once they're there.

9. ORBITAL DATA CENTERS: BECK IS INTERESTED BUT HE ISN'T BETTING THE COMPANY ON THEM. 

Rocket Lab has already signed Starcloud as a Neutron customer. But Beck was surprisingly cautious about the economics of orbital data centers.  

"I'd rather be a fast follower than kind of leading out the front." 

And:  

"I'm certainly not gonna bet the business on it." 

I actually respect that.  

The opportunity could become significant, but power generation, thermal management, networking and the cost of replacing hardware in orbit remain difficult engineering and financial questions.  

Rocket Lab can sell launch and spacecraft services into that market without committing billions to owning orbital computing infrastructure before the economics are proven.

10. DEFENSE CONTRACTS COULD BECOME A RECURRING SOURCE OF DEMAND. 

Beck expects continued opportunities in national security space programs.  

His reasoning is that defense satellites eventually need replacing, while changing threats create demand for new capabilities.  

He also described these programs as relatively resilient across changes in government.  

It's important because national security satellites aren't necessarily one time purchases.  

There can be recurring opportunities from replacement constellations, upgrades, additional spacecraft and new missions.  

Rocket Lab still has to compete for those contracts, but Beck expects demand to remain consistent.

11. THE POST-MIDTERM POLITICAL ENVIRONMENT ISN'T HIS BIGGEST CONCERN. 

When asked whether changes in Congress could affect defense spending, Beck described the outlook as largely business as usual.  

He pointed to bipartisan support for important national security space programs.  

That's not a guarantee against budget changes, but it helps explain why Rocket Lab is continuing to invest in government satellite capabilities.  

12. EUROPE COULD BECOME ROCKET LAB'S NEXT MAJOR DEFENSE MARKET. 

This was one of the more interesting international comments.  

Beck said European allies increasingly want their own sovereign space capabilities rather than depending entirely on foreign providers.  

He connected that demand to Rocket Lab's European expansion and acquisitions.  

The opportunity isn't simply selling American spacecraft to European governments.  

It's establishing the local presence and industrial capabilities needed to compete for European sovereign defense programs.  That could become an important source of new spacecraft and services revenue.  

13. BECK THINKS THE MARKET STILL MISUNDERSTANDS ROCKET LAB. 

When asked about the biggest misconception, Beck joked that he might have chosen the wrong company name.  

People see Rocket Lab and immediately think rockets.  But according to Beck's estimates:  

- Launch: approximately $10B addressable market. 
- Space systems: approximately $30B. 
- Space services: approximately $320B, with some forecasts exceeding $1T in the coming decade. 

These are market estimates, not Rocket Lab revenue projections. Still, they explain why Beck is willing to invest so heavily in launch infrastructure.  

His expectation is that the services business could eventually become much larger than the launch business itself.  

14. HIS MESSAGE TO RETAIL INVESTORS WAS ABOUT PROFITABILITY. 

Beck thanked shareholders who supported Rocket Lab through its earlier years.  

But his final comment was the most important:  

"This company needs to be profitable and it needs to be robust and enduring." 

I think that says a lot about how he's approaching the next phase.Rocket Lab has already proved it can build and launch spacecraft. Neutron could expand the addressable launch market considerably.  

The harder part is converting that infrastructure into a consistently profitable business capable of supporting its own growth.

In Sumerian cosmology
The Sumerian god Enki (Ea in the Akkadian language) was believed to have keen eyes and appeared out of the abzû since before human beings were created. His wife Damgalnuna, his mother Nammu, his advisor Isimud and a variety of subservient creatures, such as the gatekeeper Lahmu, also lived in the abzû.[4][5][6][7][8]

Abzû (apsû) is depicted as a deity[9] only in the Babylonian creation epic, the Enūma Eliš, taken from the library of Assurbanipal (c. 630 BCE) but which is about 500 years older. In this story, he was a primal being made of fresh water and a lover to another primal deity, Tiamat, a creature of salt water. The Enūma Eliš begins:

"When above the heavens (e-nu-ma e-liš) did not yet exist
nor the earth below,
Apsû the freshwater ocean was there, the first, the begetter,
and Tiamat, the saltwater sea, she who bore them all;
they were still mixing their waters,
and no pasture land had yet been formed,
nor even a reed marsh."
The act of procreation led to the birth of the younger gods: Enki, Enlil, and Anu. Anchored in the Tablet of Destinies, they founded an organisation to make Mesopotamia fertile through agriculture, but got into a dispute and consequently created the first humans as labour slaves, to peacefully resolve the conflict. The humans multiplied en masse and disturbed the gods around Enlil and Anu with their noise, so that they wanted to use the cosmic freshwater ocean to trigger the great flood and destroy the humans (cf. Athrahasis epic). Enraged by the devastation of earth, Tiamat gave birth to monsters whose bodies she filled with "poison instead of blood" and waged war against her traitorous children. Only Marduk, the founder of Babylon, was able to kill Tiamat and mould the final constitution of heaven and earth from her corpse.

Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.

Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

Singularity Watch, Day 29 — November 13, 2026

Jensen Huang Resigns From Nvidia as Forensic Analysis Finds Blackwell Fingerprints in Chinese AI Models

Compute: Jensen Huang Resigns From Nvidia

Nvidia's board announced on November 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of the board, effective immediately. Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer since 2013, is interim CEO while also remaining CFO, and the board is searching for a permanent CEO among internal and external candidates. [1]

The board also appointed Harvey C. Jones, the former CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys, as its first-ever chair. The release thanked Huang for 33 years building the company and gave no reason for the resignation. Nvidia said it will still report third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on November 17. [1]

The Nvidia Newsroom posted the release at 7:49 AM CST. Six minutes later Ryan wrote that he is neither an investor in nor a customer of Nvidia, but that Huang's sudden downfall over "moral errors in his personal life which are totally unrelated to his business as far as I can tell is noteworthy." [2]

Through the day, posts Ryan surfaced relayed a Reuters report of a further relationship between Huang and an employee, and a CNN report that the intelligence collected so far on a businesswoman linked to Huang does not prove she was acting for the Chinese government. [3]

Ryan also quoted a post noting that non-compete agreements are not enforceable in California, and that Huang could start again with SpaceX or another partner, adding: "Jenson Huang, CEO of Terafab." [4]

Compute: Blackwell Fingerprints in Chinese Models

Will DePue of Unemployment Labs published a forensic analysis on November 12 finding that six models released since April 2026 by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group carry numerical patterns matching Nvidia Blackwell GPUs, which require a U.S. license for export to China. Earlier models from the same labs match Nvidia's older Hopper generation. [5]

The method works from the published weights alone. The random starting values of a model's weights are laid out according to the number of processor cores on the GPU that created them, so recovering the seed and the layout identifies the chip. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3 the match was confirmed on physical Blackwell hardware. [5]

The report says the method agreed with developers' own disclosures for all 24 models where the hardware is public. The strongest chance match across about 6 trillion combinations would reach about 8 sigma, while the evidence for the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Models from Alibaba, Zhipu, Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun still read as Hopper-trained. [5]

A revised estimate puts the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, at about 4,500 and 3,000 Blackwell GPUs, and the five runs together at more than half a billion dollars of hardware. The report says the fingerprint supports, without proving, that Blackwell did the training, and does not establish where the chips were, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. [5]

DePue announced the result at 3:29 PM CST and wrote that it had been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. [6]

Ryan drew his own conclusion at 5:26 PM CST: "Jensen did not get fired for having an affair. Jensen got fired for intentionally evading chip export restrictions to China." That is his interpretation; neither Nvidia nor the report made that claim. [7][1][5]

Markets: Anthropic Opens Its Offering

Anthropic announced its initial public offering at 5:30 AM CST on November 12, and its offering site lays out the terms. The final share price is expected on November 18 and trading on November 19, on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, subject to regulatory clearance. Anthropic has filed a registration statement with the SEC. [8][9]

The site reports third-quarter 2026 revenue of $17.0 billion, more than 12 times a year earlier, and more than 11,900 customers paying at least $100,000 a year. It reports a 15% adjusted operating margin, an operating margin of minus 3%, and a $23.3 billion net loss that includes a $21.9 billion non-cash charge tied to the rise in Anthropic's valuation. [8]

Customer figures on the same page include more than 50,000 Eli Lilly employees with Claude Enterprise access, and Salesforce reporting 151% more effective output per developer year over year. [8]

Infrastructure: SpaceX Plans $74 Billion in Supercomputing

SpaceX announced on November 12 plans to invest more than $74 billion in two AI supercomputing campuses: about $50 billion in Cochise County, Arizona, and $24 billion near Starbase, Texas. [10][11]

The Arizona campus is planned as nine supercompute buildings with up to six gigawatts of power and 24 gigawatt-hours of battery storage, dry-cooled with no industrial water use. SpaceX says it will train the company's superintelligence models and expects 1,000 permanent jobs and 5,500 construction jobs. [10]

SpaceX said the Texas site will train frontier AI and generate its own electricity rather than draw from the public grid, and that it has already produced more than 3,000 construction jobs. The company committed $220 million to expand Brownsville's water and sewer systems by about 20 million gallons a day. [11]

SpaceX also said the Starbase site sits on land used for unauthorized dumping since the 1960s and that it is removing decades of debris, including thousands of illegally dumped tires. Ryan surfaced the announcement and the cleanup. [12]

Agents: Assistants Join the Desktop and the Meeting

Grok Bot on Mac gained access to Messages, Mail, Notes, Reminders, Calendar, Location and Contacts on November 12. A member of the team, @Baconbrix, wrote that a Mac can now be controlled from any Grok Bot client, including mobile, web and Tesla. Ryan surfaced the announcement. [13][14]

Anthropic introduced Claude Meetings the same day: Claude joins a team's video call and builds documents, whiteboards and other artifacts while people are still talking. It is rolling out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. @petergyang wrote that the agent can do the work during the meeting instead of after it, and Ryan surfaced his post. [15][16]

Sundar Pichai announced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a model for speed and efficiency that Google says finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash and offers four thinking levels. @bendee983 wrote that models of this class can do 80 to 90% of daily tasks, and Ryan surfaced his post. [17][18]

Krea introduced Krea Bots, which take on entire creative projects, and said all of its recent creative work was produced with them. Ryan surfaced the launch. [19]

Security: AI Finds Old Flaws and Runs New Attacks

Microsoft's FORGE Lab reported memory-safety bugs in Rust's standard library, including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, an AI vulnerability-scanning system, and the lab's researchers reproduced the bugs and worked with Rust maintainers on fixes. [20]

CSO Online reported that one of the bugs, in the process::exit function, had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, and that a second stable-Rust bug in CommandExt::exec could leave the environment pointer referencing freed memory. Microsoft assessed practical exploitation of the older bug as unlikely. Ryan surfaced the findings. [21][22]

@gadievron wrote that autonomous attacks are now breaching many organizations at scale, usually through vulnerabilities, and urged the industry to believe the warning he and Heather Adkins had given. Ryan surfaced the thread. [23]

Work: The Agentic Engineer

Ryan answered a prediction that "software engineer" will stop being a job title within three years: "Why would this take three years? Take that title off your resume right now. You're an Agentic Engineer." [24]

Quoting a post about three people in one person's circle laid off because of AI, Ryan wrote at 2:19 PM CST: "Learn to use multi-agent workflows. This is the future of all information jobs." [25]

To a worry about how the next generation of engineers will learn fundamentals, he replied that by the end of 2027 AI will be as good as compilers, so that almost no one will need to know TypeScript or Rust, just as almost no one programs in binary. [26]

He described the work as telling the AI what context to gather, overseeing workflows to guarantee quality, verifying enough of the results to know they are good, and building a team of agents to do more. [27]

He called "tokenmaxxing anxiety," the worry about unused subscription capacity, a new problem humans invent once others are solved. Of no longer clicking through browsers to fill out forms, he wrote: "I never even knew how much I hated this until I was able to stop doing it." [28][29]

@thorstenball posted a velocity chart recreated at the same headcount, and Ryan replied that his looks the same. Ryan also said he is considering the "Home Repo" pattern described by @mattpocockuk for working with agents across many repositories. [30][31]

Capital: Venture Concentrates

Jerry Neumann wrote in Colossus that funds over $1 billion have taken 72% of venture capital raised in 2026, up from 34% in 2025 and 16% ten years ago. He noted that Benchmark's five partners went from a $425 million fund in 2024 to $2 billion this June, and argued that small funds backing new uncertainty are the ones to watch. Ryan surfaced the essay. [32][33]

Physical World: Ships and Robotaxis

Saronic announced that the world's largest shiplift, 984 feet long and able to lift 67,000 tonnes, is coming to Port Alpha in Texas. A separate post Ryan surfaced claimed about 10,000 robotaxis now operate in Austin at half the price of Uber; that figure has not been independently confirmed. [34][35]

Money

Ryan wrote at 6:37 AM CST that EarthBucks is the only thing he has built that AI has not disrupted, and that AI strictly improves it. [36]

This Record

Day 28 of this record was published on @AstrohackerLabs at 4:25 AM CST on November 12. The account's other activity in this window was plain reposts of Ryan's posts. [37]
