text:
Before a single duck had eaten anything, the whole yard already knew something was about to happen.

I keep coming back to that, because nothing in the first seconds of this video looks like an event. There is a wide black tub sitting on a ledge of rounded stones. There is a yellow bucket off to one side and a garden hose snaking across the wet ground. And there are the ducks, white ones, a few black ones, one black-and-white one with a red mask of bare skin around its eyes, drifting around the stones the way birds do when they are pretending not to wait.

But they are waiting. Every head is turned the same way. The tub is empty, or nearly so, a shallow slick of water in the bottom and nothing else, and still the birds orient toward it like iron filings toward a magnet.

So the first question is a strange one. What do they know that we don't?

Here is the answer that took me a while to appreciate: they know everything. They know the tub. They know the bucket. They know the person who is just out of frame, and the sound his feet make, and what the sequence of small noises means. To a stranger, this is a quiet morning scene in a farmyard. To the flock, it is a language they have been reading for a long time, and they are reading it fluently.

Then the water in the tub changes, and so does the yard.

Eggs go in. A little cluster of them, pale ovals tumbling into the water, with bright yellow smears among them that turn the dark bottom of the tub into something almost festive. One egg slides away from the group and floats on its own, off to the right, like it doesn't want to be part of what comes next.

If you only half-watch, you might think this is the whole recipe: eggs and water, a duck's breakfast. It is not even close to finished. And the next thing that happens is the part I would not have predicted.

A black plastic bag appears at the top of the frame. Two hands tilt it, and what comes out is not grain, not whole corn, not scraps. It is a pale, pinkish-white powder, a thick fall of it, pouring into the tub in a soft column and clouding the water as it lands. The powder hits the surface and billows up in a haze, the way flour does when you drop it from too high.

The ducks do not wait politely for any of this to finish. A black-and-white bird with that red face leans in from the left edge of the frame, its head level with the rim of the tub. Another red-masked head appears from the right. They are close enough to the falling powder that you can see the dust drift past their beaks. Neither of them takes anything. Neither of them moves away.

That restraint is the first small mystery in this story, and it is easy to miss. Hungry animals, a pile of food, a tub within beak's reach, and yet the birds hold at the edge. The rim of that tub is a border, and every duck in the yard is respecting it.

Why?

I can only tell you what the video lets me see, and I want to be careful about that, because the temptation with animal footage is to supply thoughts the animals never announced. I do not know what the ducks are thinking. I know what they are doing. They stand around a container that is being filled, and they do not dive in until the filling is done. That is a behavior, not a mind-reading, and behaviors can be explained in more than one way.

One explanation is simple conditioning: in a place where food arrives on a schedule and in a ritual, animals learn that the ritual is the food. The pour, the mixing, the carrying are all part of one chain, and the chain ends in eating. Birds who have lived inside that chain would learn to stay close and stay out of the way until the last link.

Another explanation is about the person. Whoever is standing at that tub has his hands in the middle of everything, and a bird that rushes the container risks a bump, a swat, a spill. There is a cost to being too eager. Over time, a flock tends to find the distance at which closeness pays and crowding does not.

Neither explanation needs the ducks to be doing anything more mysterious than learning. But I'll admit that when you watch it, it doesn't feel like learning. It feels like manners.

The mixing is when the tub finally turns into something.

The powder, the eggs and the water go from three separate things into one, and the transformation is quick. A hand goes in, and what was a milky cloud becomes a thick, sandy paste the color of wet cardboard. At one point you can see the surface of it clearly: a pale, grainy mass, studded with yellow flecks and ragged chunks, packed against the sides of the tub. It looks like batter. It looks, honestly, like something you would be a little afraid to taste.

And right there, the video's own caption does its quiet work. Across the top of the frame, in plain white letters, are the words "Nutritious animal feed." That is all it says. No numbers, no ingredient list, no claims about what the mix does. Just a statement of intent, laid over a tub of paste while a duck stretches its neck toward it.

I find that caption more interesting than it first seems, precisely because of how little it tells you. It names the purpose and leaves out everything that would let you check it. We can see eggs go in. We can see a powder go in. We cannot see what the powder is, how much of anything there is, or whether any of it is, in fact, a better meal than what these birds would otherwise eat. The video asks you to take "nutritious" as a premise and watch what the people and birds do with it.

So let me do what the video does. Let me take the premise as given, and watch.

The tub is not where the eating happens. That is the second surprise.

You would think, from the way the ducks crowd the ledge, that the meal would be served right there. But the next shift in the video is a shift in scale. The camera pulls back, the sky opens up behind the fence, a tidy house with a red tile roof comes into view, and a man stands at the tub in a white T-shirt and a deep red patterned wrap-style garment, the kind of printed cloth that looks like it was made to be worn in warm weather. He is bending over the tub, and the ducks have closed around him so tightly that he has to work among their bodies.

There are more birds than the first frames suggested. A dozen at least, maybe many more past the edges of the shot, white and cream and black, some of them with those red faces turned toward whatever his hands are doing. They press against his legs and against each other. A black bird at the left edge of the frame stands almost in the tub's shadow, patient. A white duck perches on the ledge itself, level with the paste, leaning in from above.

And he is not hurried. That is what stands out. A person surrounded by that many hungry animals could easily rush, or shoo them off, or lose his temper. He does none of it. He stands, he bends, he scoops. The whole motion has the unhurried rhythm of someone who has done this so many times that the crowd is just part of the weather.

Then comes the bucket.

It is an orange one, and it enters the story as a vehicle. The paste goes into it, and from that moment the meal stops being a scene and becomes a journey. The man lifts the bucket, turns, and begins to walk, and the ducks, who had been a ring around the tub, reorganize themselves into something like a procession.

This is the part of the video that I think deserves a slower look, because it shows how much the flock understands without being told. Nothing in the frame suggests a call or a command. The man just starts moving with the food, and the birds fall in around him, ahead of him, behind him, under his feet. Some of them trot. Some of them flap a little for speed. They are not following him exactly. They are following the bucket, and the man happens to be what it hangs from.

When a person walks across a yard and a crowd of animals simply understands where he is going, you are watching something that cannot be filmed directly. You are watching a relationship that has been built out of ten thousand repeated moments. The video can only show you the result.

And the result is a walk to a different part of the property entirely.

The scenery changes. Gone are the rounded stones and the green fabric screen and the hose. Now there is bamboo everywhere: bamboo fencing, bamboo posts, a floor made of narrow bamboo slats laid with gaps between them, like a long wooden grate. It is a structure designed by people who know a great deal about keeping things dry and clean in a place where it rains, and it looks like it has been used heavily and cared for.

The man, in his bright sarong-like trousers and flip-flops, steps along it carrying the heavy black container, and you can see the angle of his back as he leans away from the weight. The floor under him is not the floor the ducks are used to. A couple of birds have gotten ahead of him and are already standing on the slats, looking back.

On that slatted platform, there is a small tray. It is shallow, a pale rectangle sitting by itself on the bamboo, holding a modest scattering of crumbly feed. And next to it, alone for a moment, stands one black-and-white duck.

I want to stay on that image, because it is the quietest and, to me, the strangest in the whole video.

Here is a bird with a tray of food at its feet and a whole flock about to arrive, and it is just standing there. The other ducks have not arrived. The man has not set down the container yet. This one duck, a pied muscovy with a splash of dark feathers and a white chest, is positioned beside the tray like a guard, or like a first guest who showed up early to a party and doesn't know what to do with their hands.

Is it guarding? Is it just looking? The honest answer is that I can't tell, and I think anyone who claims to be certain is guessing. What I can say is that it holds a position, and that the position is closer to the tray than anyone else's. And I can say that a moment later, the room around it fills up.

Behind the bamboo fence, there is more.

If you look past the slatted floor, through the vertical gaps in the fence, you can make out another pen, and in it a pale crowd of birds packed shoulder to shoulder. It is easy to overlook, a smear of white against the brown. But it changes the scale of the story. This is not a handful of backyard ducks being fed a treat. This looks like a place where a large number of birds live, and the tub, the bucket and the walk across the yard are one part of a much bigger daily operation.

That matters, because it reframes the first image. When I told you that the ducks at the tub seemed to know what was coming, I was describing one flock in one corner of something larger. The knowing is not a trick performed by a few pets. It is the working knowledge of an entire farm, repeated across countless mornings.

Now the man sets the food down, and the real eating begins.

It happens at a trough made from what looks like a long length of split log, a plain hollow in a wooden beam, resting low to the ground. Fine, crumbly feed lies along it. And here the ducks finally do what they have been holding back from doing since the first frame.

They go in all at once, and yet not chaotically. White heads, long-necked and orange-billed, line up along the length of the beam. A few of the birds have those fleshy red patches around the eyes and base of the bill, the feature that makes muscovy ducks look like they are wearing a small, slightly alarming mask. Their bills work along the surface of the wood in quick, dabbing motions, and bits of the mixture fly up and settle on feathers and on the ground.

Look closely at the wood and you can see the feed has dried into a coarse, sandy crumb. This is not the soupy paste from the tub. Somewhere between the tub and the trough, the meal has changed texture, and I can't tell from the video how. Maybe the mixture was spread out and left to firm up. Maybe what ends up in the trough is a different preparation altogether. I'm not going to guess. What I notice is only this: the thing that was a wet batter in the first scene is a dry crumble in the last. The farm has a process, and the video only lets us see its edges.

And here is something that I think the footage captures better than any caption could.

Ducks do not eat like chickens. A chicken pecks. A duck works its bill along a surface and sifts. The whole front of the bill is a sensitive instrument, packed with nerve endings, and a feeding duck is constantly reading what it finds. It is a more careful way of eating than it looks, and it explains why the birds stay at the trough so long, heads bobbing, each one lost in its own small patch of wood.

Ducks also like water close to their food. Anyone who has kept them knows the habit: take a mouthful, dip the bill, take another. The whole yard in this video is built around that. There is a channel of water along the base of the stone ledge. There is the hose. The tub itself began as a water tub. The people who set up this farm clearly understand that a duck's meal and a duck's drink are one continuous act, and they have arranged the space so the two are never far apart.

I did not notice that at first. It took watching the video a second time, with the ducks in mind rather than the person, to see how much of the architecture is arranged around the birds' own habits.

Then comes the moment I find myself rewinding.

Midway through the eating, there is a fraction of a second where the crowd shifts. A white duck stretches its neck and shoulders a black one aside. The black one, a glossy bird whose feathers show green and blue where the light catches them, does not fight. It steps back, repositions, and finds a different spot at the same beam. A third bird takes the gap, and the whole thing is over before you can register it.

This is what social life in a flock looks like when it works. There is a pecking order, and it is mostly invisible, because the birds mostly agree on it. Every small shove is a negotiation that has already been settled. The black duck has not been defeated. It has simply understood, long ago, how the room is arranged.

You can see the same arrangement in how the different colors mix. White birds, dark birds and pied birds share the trough without separating by color. If there is a hierarchy, it does not follow plumage. It follows something we cannot see from here: age, size, temperament, who arrived first this morning.

I keep wanting to ask what this says about the farm, and I want to be careful, because I can only read what the footage gives me. But there is one thing it gives me clearly: these animals are not afraid.

That is the quiet truth of the whole video. At no point does a bird flinch from the man. At no point does the flock scatter when he moves. Ducks are, by their nature, wary of large moving things. They flee, they bunch, they bolt. Here they walk between his feet. They stand at the edge of the tub while his hands move above them. One bird sits on the ledge above the mixing and leans over it as if looking over his shoulder.

An animal that is comfortable around a person did not get that way in a day. It is the end of a long chain of days in which a hand meant food and a footstep meant something good. When you see a flock that follows a bucket across a yard, you are seeing the sum of a thousand uneventful, unremarkable, repeated acts of care. Nobody filmed those. They are just the reason this one minute looks the way it does.

So let's go back to the very first image and see if it looks different.

An empty tub. A group of ducks waiting. At the start, it seemed like a scene about hunger, birds in a state of wanting. But after watching the rest, I don't think hunger is the right word. Hunger is frantic. These birds are not frantic. They are expectant, which is a calmer and more specific thing. They are waiting for something they have good reason to believe is coming.

That difference changes the meaning of the entire opening. The stillness around the tub, the restraint at the rim, the way the red-faced birds held their heads just short of the falling powder: none of that is a sign of deprivation. It is a sign of trust, or at least of reliable routine, which in the life of an animal may amount to the same thing.

I want to say that more precisely, because it is easy to romanticize it.

I cannot see inside a duck, and I won't pretend to. I can't tell you whether any of these birds feel anything like gratitude, or affection, or even a recognizable version of trust. The word I keep reaching for might be the wrong one. What I can tell you is that the birds behave as if the pattern is safe, and that they have organized their movements around the belief, if "belief" is even the word, that the person at the tub will do what he always does.

Maybe that is all trust ever was. Not a feeling, but a prediction held so steadily that you stop bracing against the alternative.

There is one more detail about these particular birds that quietly deepens the scene, and it has to do with how they sound, or rather how little.

The ducks with the red faces are muscovies, a breed that behaves differently from the mallard-derived ducks most people picture. Muscovies are known for being unusually quiet. They do not quack the way a cartoon duck does. Their voices are closer to soft trills and low hisses, and often they communicate by posture alone: a lifted crest, a bobbing head, the angle of the body. A farmyard full of them can look like a crowd of loud animals and still be nearly silent.

That changes how I read the crowd at the tub. If these were noisy birds, the scene would be a clamor, and I would be tempted to call the waiting impatience. Instead the language of the flock is mostly visual. Heads turn together. Bodies lean. A bird steps back and another steps in. The whole negotiation of who stands where and who eats when is conducted in a medium most of us barely notice, which is one reason it feels so calm.

It also explains the restraint at the rim of the tub. A species that settles things with posture is a species with a great deal of practice at reading small signals, and the person at the center of the circle is giving off plenty of them.

Notice, too, how the mixture reaches them. Nothing in the video is dropped from above or thrown across the ground. It is carried, set down and left in a vessel designed for sharing. That small decision, a long wooden trough rather than a scatter of feed, does a lot of quiet work. A trough means every bird gets a place along an edge. It means the food stays off the dirt. It means the stronger ducks can take the middle without ever making the weaker ones leave, because there is room at the ends.

I do not know whether the farmer thought about any of this, or whether the trough was simply the thing that was available. But the effect is visible: a crowd of different sizes and colors, eating shoulder to shoulder at a single beam, with no one driven off.

Now step back and ask what first misled me about this clip, because I think it is the same thing that misleads most people who watch it.

It looks like a video about food. The tub, the powder and the paste, the caption announcing something nutritious: every visual cue points at the meal. Even the title of the clip frames it that way, with a farmer, a feeding time and a promise of high nutrition. You watch expecting a lesson in what to feed ducks.

And then you realize the food is the least interesting thing in it. We never learn what is in the powder. We never see a number. The recipe, if there is one, is withheld. What the video actually shows, once you stop waiting for the recipe, is a relationship: people and animals sharing a daily choreography so familiar to both that neither has to explain it.

That is the quiet reversal in the middle of the story. You came for the feed and you stayed for the behavior. The caption says one thing, and the footage says something larger.

I find that these are often the clips worth passing on. Not the ones with the dramatic rescue or the miracle ending, but the ones in which an ordinary hour contains more than it claims to, if you are willing to watch it twice.

The final shot is the one that surprised me most, because nothing happens in it.

The ducks are still at the trough, still eating. A few dark birds sit low against the bamboo. A white duck stands in the foreground, turned away, its feathers a little ruffled. And in the background, the man is sweeping.

He holds a broom with a blue handle and a head of stiff, dry sticks, the traditional kind, and he drags it across the packed dirt in long, easy strokes. His white T-shirt, with its printed logo, is a bright patch under the dark roof beams. He is not looking at the camera. He is not looking at the ducks. He is clearing the ground.

I think that is the most honest moment in the video. Everything before it is spectacle, the pour of powder, the swirl of paste, the crowd of birds at the beam. This is the part nobody would put in a headline. It is the ordinary maintenance that makes the spectacle possible: after the feeding, you clean up. The yard has to be ready for tomorrow.

And there is something a little humbling in that. The meal, the thing that looked like the point of the video, is already over. The cleanup, the part that seems like an afterthought, is the part that goes on. It is the daily labor underneath the daily meal, and the birds are eating over it as though it were part of the landscape.

Consider what it takes to make a minute like this one. Someone has to buy or gather the ingredients, lift the heavy tub onto its ledge, mix the batter by hand, carry the weight across the yard, set it down, sweep up afterward and then do it all again the next day. None of those steps is dramatic. Taken singly, none of them would be worth filming. Yet together they make up the thing the ducks actually depend on, and the clip, almost by accident, preserves it.

There is a lesson in that for anyone who watches animal videos looking for the big moment. Sometimes the big moment is the absence of one: a flock that does not panic, a meal that arrives when it should, a person who is exactly where the birds expect him to be.

A few things I cannot tell you about this video, and I think it's worth being honest about them.

I can't tell you where it was filmed. The tiled roofs and the printed cloth and the bamboo suggest a warm, humid part of the world, and the clip's own label offers other guesses, but I don't know, and a guess stated as a fact would be a small dishonesty.

I can't tell you what the powder is, or how much of it goes into a batch, or whether the mixture really does what the caption says. I can't tell you how many ducks live on the farm, how old they are, how long this routine has been running, or whether the man in the video is the owner, a worker, a family member. I can't tell you his name, and I don't think it matters.

What I can tell you is what the clip gives me when I look at it slowly: a group of animals that wait without panic, a person who works without hurry, a set of arrangements built carefully around how ducks really behave, and a meal that gets made, carried and eaten in about a minute of footage.

There is a version of this video that is just a nice clip of ducks eating, and that version is perfectly good. People will scroll past it with a small smile and a half-second of warmth. But I think the more interesting version is the one underneath it, the one about how much of animal life depends on the dull, patient reliability of someone showing up.

Ducks do not know the word "farm." They don't know the word "routine," or "care," or "nutritious." What they know is a sound, a bucket, a pair of feet crossing a yard. For them, the whole structure of a good life is those small signals, repeated until they stop being signals and start being the shape of the day.

And somewhere in that shape, a black-and-white bird stands beside a nearly bare tray, waiting.

The tray fills, as it always seems to. That bird had no way of knowing that for certain. It stood there anyway, close to the place where the food would land, as though the answer had been decided long before the powder ever hit the water.

Watch the opening seconds again after the ending, and the empty tub no longer looks empty. It looks like a stage waiting for a cast that has already arrived. Every bird in the first frame is already standing in the right place, facing the right way, early. They had read the morning correctly before anything had been poured, and the rest of the video is simply the world slowly catching up to what they knew.

I think that is what stays with me. Not the pour or the paste or the crowd at the trough. Just that one patient duck at the edge of a bamboo floor, holding its place, in no hurry at all.

It was not waiting for the food. It was waiting for the person who always brings it, which is a much older kind of hope.

The Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) have appointed Clark | AECOM, a joint venture of Clark Construction Group (@ClarkBuilds) and AECOM (@AECOM), to the construction team for the NFL club's new 70,000-person fixed-roof stadium in Wyandotte County, Kansas, which is due to open in 2031.

The stadium accounts for $3 billion of a $4.5 billion investment programme in Kansas, which also covers a $300 million practice facility and headquarters in Olathe and $1.2 billion of private real estate development around both sites. Design work rests with MANICA and HNTB (@HNTBCorp), and sitework on the stadium site is scheduled to start in 2027.

Mark Donovan, President of the Kansas City Chiefs, said: “We are excited to have the Clark | AECOM team join us for our transformational stadium project that will benefit the entire region.”

He added: “They understand our vision and have the expertise required for this scale of project, and we look forward to collaborating with them as we prepare for construction to begin.”

Lee DeLong, CEO of Clark Group, said: “This project represents an exciting new era for Kansas City, poised to transform the sports and entertainment experience for the region, and serve as a powerful catalyst for economic growth and community connection.”

Ken Johnson, Executive Vice President and Sports Market leader of AECOM Hunt (@AECOMHunt), said: “NFL stadium projects present some of the most complex challenges in our industry, and that’s where our team thrives.”

He added: “We bring decades of experience, innovative thinking, and a relentless commitment to delivering world-class facilities that spur job creation and fuel the economic engines of communities nationwide.”

text:
Is the AI bubble actually deflating, or is the market simply becoming more realistic about AI valuations?

Anthropic’s upcoming IPO is an interesting case to watch.

A few weeks ago, reports suggested that Anthropic could be targeting a valuation of around $2 trillion. But following the recent tech market selloff, some investors reportedly reconsidered that valuation, with discussions falling toward the $1.1T–$1.3T range.

There was also an initial reported IPO price range of $70–$80, which was later retracted. Subsequent reports discussed an updated $70–$78 range.

These figures come from different stages of reporting, so they shouldn’t be treated as one confirmed set of final IPO terms.

So, is this the beginning of an AI bubble deflating?

I think it’s more interesting to look at this as a possible shift in market expectations.

AI is still developing, and companies like Anthropic have real products and growing demand. But having strong technology doesn’t automatically justify any valuation.

Investors may be starting to look beyond the AI hype and pay closer attention to actual business performance, revenue, competition, infrastructure costs, and how long it might take for these companies to become profitable.

For traders, this is a reminder that market sentiment can change quickly. A company can have strong long-term potential while its valuation still gets reassessed.

Where does Bitget come in?

For those interested in exploring Anthropic-related exposure, Bitget offers access through its IPO Prime Public Round.

Users can subscribe using USDT or USDGO, subject to eligibility and the applicable subscription rules. After allocation, participants receive rANT, a token that provides tokenized exposure to Anthropic.

Important distinction: rANT is NOT an actual Anthropic share. It does not provide shareholder voting rights or dividends. Allocation is also subject to the round’s rules, so committing funds doesn’t guarantee full allocation.

Bitget provides access to this tokenized product. It is not Anthropic’s IPO underwriter and is not affiliated with Anthropic.

You can explore the details here in the official campaign link:
https://t.co/f2OawBfsP5

My personal takeaway here is that maybe the bigger story isn’t whether AI is losing its potential, but whether the market is finally becoming more selective about the price it puts on that potential.

Do you think this is a healthy valuation reset for the AI industry, or a sign that the AI hype is starting to cool down?

DYOR. Understand the product, fees, allocation rules, and risks before participating. Not financial advice.

Ghana’s 2027 budget puts serious money behind young people. The next question is who will help them reach it.

𝖶𝗂𝗍𝗁 29 𝖽𝖺𝗒𝗌 𝗍𝗈 𝗀𝗈, 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖦𝗋𝖾𝖾𝗇 𝖠𝗋𝗆𝗒 𝗂𝗌 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽𝗒. 

On November 12, 2026 , Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson presented the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy to Parliament, and young Ghanaians were at the centre of it.

𝖶𝗁𝖺𝗍 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖻𝗎𝖽𝗀𝖾𝗍 𝗈𝖿𝖿𝖾𝗋𝗌 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝗒𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗁 ?

The numbers are significant. The Ministry of Youth Development and Empowerment is set to receive GH¢3.5 billion, with GH¢2 billion of that earmarked for youth employment and skills development. A further GH¢200 million is allocated to the National Youth Authority.

The government also plans to amend the Earmarked Funds Capping and Realignment Act so that Communications Service Tax revenue for youth employment and apprenticeships is no longer capped. That move is expected to free up an additional GH¢1 billion.

Alongside it, the Youth Employment Act will be amended and modernised so that the many youth employment programmes work together instead of in isolation.

𝖳𝗁𝖾 𝗌𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖾 𝗈𝖿 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝖼𝗁𝖺𝗅𝗅𝖾𝗇𝗀𝖾 𝖾𝗑𝗉𝗅𝖺𝗂𝗇𝗌 𝗍𝗁𝖾 𝗎𝗋𝗀𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗒.

The Finance Minister put the number of young Ghanaians who are not in employment, education or training at 1.34 million, and warned that it could climb to about 1.7 million over the next four years if nothing changes.

The budget’s answer is the US$10 billion New Economy programme, running from 2027 to 2030. Where a budget stops and leadership starts.

A budget sets the direction and releases the money. It cannot, on its own, make sure a young person in a small town knows a programme exists, understands how to apply, or gets a response when something goes wrong. That gap between a promise in Parliament and a result in a town/branch/Constituency is where the Youth Wing matters.

This is the gap @okai_mintah has built his campaign for National Youth Organiser around. As Chairperson of the National Youth Working Committee and Head of Operations for the Youth Wing’s 2024 campaign, he has years of experience in the party’s national youth structures. His pledges fit the moment closely.

𝖠 𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗉𝗈𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝖾 𝖣𝖾𝗌𝗄 𝗍𝗁𝖺𝗍 𝗅𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗌.

Okai Mintah has promised a desk that receives complaints, concerns and requests from Youth Wing members and makes sure they are acted on promptly. When government programmes expand, young people need a clear channel to raise questions and be heard.

Engagement all year, not just in election season. He has said that youth mobilisation should go beyond election-year activity, with permanent engagement between the party and young people. 

A four-year economic programme calls for the same kind of steady, sustained effort. Structures that are strong and properly resourced. 

@okai_mintah has committed to strengthening and adequately resourcing the party’s mobilisation structures, so the Youth Wing can carry information, organise at the grassroots and keep young people involved from the constituency level up.

1/2

text:
IF I WERE YOU, reading this week that an AI crash is coming, I would ask one question before selling anything with AI in its name: a crash in what?

The Economist's cover shows the letters AI crumbling, and its leader is titled "Why you should expect an AI crash", with the qualification that it need not be a financial cataclysm. A Federal Reserve vice chair lists a large correction in equities among the risks if AI returns disappoint. Axios calls it the industry's week from hell. Nvidia has lost its founder and nearly a third of its value in five weeks.

I do not expect a collapse of AI. That is a narrower claim than it sounds, and a different one from this week's covers. Every technological revolution meets the same two characters: the enthusiast who believes every price is justified and the pessimist who mistakes a falling price for the end of an industry. AI now has plenty of both. Here is the record, from filings, surveys and market data, then the argument, then the part of the bear case I think is right. Facts are stated as facts. The interpretation is mine and is labelled as such.

FOUR THINGS HIDING IN ONE WORD

When someone predicts a collapse, I want to know which balance sheet or which behaviour they mean.

One: a collapse in valuations, what investors will pay for the earnings. A wonderful business can be a poor investment at the wrong price.

Two: a collapse in a financing model. A company with an impressive product can still run out of cash if its commitments grow faster than its ability to fund them.

Three: an infrastructure bust. Capacity built in the wrong place, at the wrong price, ahead of demand, or without the power to run it.

Four: a collapse in adoption. Customers stop using the technology because it is too expensive, too unreliable or not useful enough.

The first is not a forecast: for the leading stock it has already happened. The second and third are real risks and I will not talk them down. The fourth is the only one that would end the AI economy, and it is the one for which I can find no evidence. The first three can happen without the fourth, and a financial crash can be deep and painful while the technology keeps spreading. My thesis is a judgment about adoption. It is not a promise about anyone's return.

THE WEEK

On Thursday 12 November Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director of Nvidia, effective immediately, after 33 years. He had acknowledged an extramarital affair; the woman, according to press reports citing American intelligence, is suspected of being a Chinese asset, and a second relationship, with an executive who reported to him, was reported on Wednesday night. Nvidia had said it was examining whether he had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort". A suspicion is not a finding, and I will treat it as a suspicion.

Colette Kress, chief financial officer since 2013, is interim chief executive and remains chief financial officer. Harvey Jones becomes the first chair the board has ever had. There is no named successor.

The shares fell as much as 14%, to $148.80, and closed at $166.19, down 4.3%. On 6 October they had closed at $239.24. That is 30.5% in five weeks and, on my arithmetic, about $1.75 trillion of market value.

VALUATIONS: ALREADY CUT

The 30.5% is three legs, not one. From 6 October to 4 November, before either shock, Nvidia lost 16%, in weeks when Alphabet and Microsoft declined to raise their capital-spending forecasts. Around the midterms it lost 7%. In the week of the scandal, 11%. About half of the fall came before the election, a fifth with it and a third this week. The scandal is the loudest leg. It is not the largest.

Look at the day itself. On the session in which the central figure of the AI trade resigned, the Nasdaq lost 0.4% and closed 4.3% above its level of a week earlier. AMD rose 5.9% and Broadcom 5.5%, while CoreWeave and other clouds that depend on Nvidia's chips fell hard. Money did not leave artificial intelligence. It changed supplier. Nvidia itself closed within a dollar of the day's high on about 748 million shares, roughly seven times its October average. Somebody bought what was sold.

Look at what the analysts did. Bernstein cut Nvidia to Market Perform and halved its target from $400 to $200, and left its earnings forecasts where they were. At least ten analysts turned more cautious in the week, by FactSet's count as reported by CNBC. What was cut was the multiple: about 14 times the next twelve months' expected earnings on TIKR's consensus, a five-year low, against a five-year average of about 36.

The arithmetic is simple. Take the $12.10 a share analysts expect over the next twelve months. At 36 times that is $436. At 14 times it is $169, roughly where the stock closed. One analyst, Dan Ives, had estimated that Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less without Huang; applied to the $186.64 of the Friday before the scandal, that is $131 to $140. On that view the founder discount is less than half taken, and I would not tell anyone the bottom is in. But if earnings estimates fell 30% at an unchanged multiple the price would be about $119, and that, a fall in the business rather than in its price, is what nobody has yet written into a forecast.

The earlier leg tells the same story. On 5 November, two days after the midterms, the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, the Philadelphia Semiconductor index about 12%, its worst day since March 2020, and roughly $2.5 trillion of market value went in a session. The trigger was not an earnings miss. Democrats had swept Congress and taken the governorships of Texas, Ohio and Georgia, and most of 41 local ballot measures on data centres had gone against the builders. That is a permitting question, and a serious one. It is not a demand question.

Cisco, the Nvidia of the last cycle, traded at well over 100 times earnings in March 2000, and the Nasdaq then lost 78% by October 2002. Nvidia trades at 14. A stock at 14 times can fall further. It cannot fall the way a stock at 100 times falls unless the earnings go.

DEMAND: WHAT DID NOT FALL

Nvidia reported $96.2 billion of revenue for its July quarter, up from $46.7 billion a year earlier, and guided to $108 billion, give or take 2%, for the quarter it reports on Tuesday.

Amazon Web Services grew 39% in the third quarter to $46 billion, Microsoft's Azure 48% to $33.2 billion, Google Cloud 103% to $30.7 billion, a figure that includes sales of Google's own chips: $110 billion in three months. A year earlier the three were growing 20%, 40% and 34%. AWS alone reports a backlog of about $578 billion.

The four largest builders guide to $720 to $740 billion of capital spending this year, with more than $1 trillion expected next year. The only cut of the season, Microsoft's from $175 to $170 billion, was attributed by the company to delayed deliveries, with customer demand still above supply. A cut caused by a shortage is the opposite of a demand problem.

ADOPTION: RISING, AT A FALLING PRICE

That is demand measured at the suppliers. The harder question is the end customer.

In McKinsey's 2026 global survey, published in August, nearly nine in ten respondents said their organisations regularly use AI in at least one business function, and the share scaling it across the enterprise rose from 38% to 44%. Four in five said it had improved their own productivity, and six in ten expect their organisations to spend more on AI over the next year. The survey covered 1,719 respondents in 97 countries. It records what respondents report and is not a census.

The same survey contains the number optimists skip. Only 37% attribute any EBIT impact to AI, unchanged from 2025, and about 6% attribute to it 5% or more of EBIT. Use has spread faster than profit. An employee can save an hour while the income statement does not move, because the workflow around that hour was never redesigned. For a chief financial officer the question is not how many people have access to a tool. It is what happens to cost, speed, quality, revenue and risk once the tool is part of the process. A successful pilot is a promising start. It is not yet a consolidated income statement.

Now a second dataset. Ramp, which tracks the spending of more than 85,000 American businesses, reports that 56.8% of them paid for AI in October, 13 points more than a year earlier. Yet spending on AI tokens grew just 1.5% across August and September combined, after 42% in July. In the four weeks to 23 October token volume rose 37% while token spend rose 9%, which implies a price per token about a fifth lower in a month. Ramp's economist attributes the slowdown mainly to price cuts and to customers learning to control their usage, not to weaker demand. Two more details belong in an honest account. The median business paying for AI spends about $16 per employee a month, while the top 1% spend about $10,000: adoption is broad and still shallow. And about 1% of businesses account for roughly 80% of what OpenAI and Anthropic earn from Ramp's customers. These are Ramp's customers, not the labs' total sales, and a few months are not a trend.

Read together, the two say something the word "crash" hides. Companies are using more AI and paying less for each unit of it. That is not a collapse in adoption. It is a collapse in price, and a falling price is a transfer: from the companies that sell intelligence to the companies that use it. This is where I part company with this week's covers. What is deflating is the price of AI, of its shares and of its tokens. What is not deflating is its use.

FINANCING: WHERE THE BEARS ARE RIGHT

The internet was real too. Being right about the technology protected no one who bought the Nasdaq in March 2000. The internet did not ask permission from a stock index to change the economy, and AI will not either. But neither owes investors a positive return. What turned that repricing into a collapse was not a shortage of users. It was the financing.

Michelle Bowman, the Fed's vice chair for supervision, said on 10 November that AI-related debt is on track to exceed $800 billion this year, and that leases, contract commitments and residual-value guarantees could add more than three times that: by arithmetic, more than $2.4 trillion of obligations, most of them absent from the balance sheets investors read. She described suppliers and hyperscalers taking stakes in their own customers as creating "the appearance of circular financing". She also attributed roughly a quarter of the excess over the Fed's inflation target to AI-related price pressures. A boom strong enough to show up in inflation is not short of demand. It is also one the central bank cannot easily rescue with lower rates.

Anthropic's amended prospectus shows third-quarter revenue of $16.96 billion, twelve times a year earlier, beside $895.4 billion of purchase and lease commitments, about thirteen times its annualised third-quarter revenue. Quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 144% to 47%, and an operating profit of $974 million became an operating loss of $567 million, largely because $5 billion of compute was bought on expensive short-term contracts. Put Ramp's falling token price next to those commitments and you have the financing question in one line: revenue per unit is falling while the bill was signed for a world of 144%.

Nvidia is not only a seller of chips. Its July-quarter filing shows $99 billion of equity investments in its own ecosystem, $25 billion more committed, and guarantees of up to $108.5 billion, of which $105 billion backs a single data-centre campus leased to an OpenAI affiliate. Kress told analysts in August that demand from the AI labs for which Nvidia expects to use its own balance sheet should be roughly a quarter of its business next year. In the same month it signed memorandums with capital providers meant to mobilise more than $500 billion of third-party money for AI infrastructure, and IFR counted more than $530 billion of commitments of all kinds at the company.

The supplier finances the customer so that the customer can buy from the supplier. Such transactions can have a legitimate commercial purpose, and their existence does not prove that sales are fictitious or that the sector is a Ponzi scheme. But an analyst should ask whether the demand would survive on similar terms without the financing. How much revenue comes from independent end customers? How concentrated is it? Can customers renew when the introductory budget disappears? Those are questions about durability and concentration, not accusations.

INFRASTRUCTURE: THE PHYSICAL LIMIT

Microsoft said roughly three quarters of the $45.2 billion of capital expenditure it reported for the September quarter, a figure that includes finance leases, went to short-lived assets, mainly CPUs and GPUs, up from about two thirds a quarter earlier. Chips that age in a few years are being financed across the industry with bonds that mature in decades. The word AI does not make a GPU exempt from economics.

And the buildings need power. The International Energy Agency projects that electricity consumption by data centres will roughly double, from about 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to about 950 in 2030, with AI-focused facilities tripling. That is a projection for all data centres, not a measurement of AI. A global total also hides the local problem: a grid connection that arrives late, a county that votes no, as most of those 41 ballots did. In the next phase, access to reliable power could matter as much as access to capital.

So there is a credible scenario in which this goes badly wrong, and it does not require anyone to stop using AI. Enterprises prove reluctant to pay enough for production use. Token prices keep falling faster than costs. Power delays several large projects. Overcapacity compresses prices just as financing becomes more expensive. Leveraged developers miss obligations and the losses spread to lenders and infrastructure owners. That would be a genuine financial crisis in parts of AI, not a change in sentiment. My belief that adoption continues is not an argument against that possibility. It is a judgment that useful applications would continue through it.

WHERE THE SCANDAL MEETS THE SYSTEM

This is my reading, not a reported fact. Huang's importance to the AI economy was never only the product roadmap. He was the person across the table in those deals: the stakes, the guarantees, the capacity promises that let suppliers and developers build ahead of orders. Key-man risk at Nvidia is a credit question before it is an engineering one. The chips for 2027 are already designed. What is not designed is who signs the next $105 billion guarantee, and on what terms.

The interim answer is a governance oddity. The executive who knows every one of those commitments best is now chief executive and chief financial officer at once. For customers and lenders that is continuity. For a board supervising $108.5 billion of guarantees, it is one person in two chairs that exist to check each other.

And there is a governance fact that predates the scandal. Until Thursday Nvidia's board had never had a chair. Its chief executive had, by Bernstein's count, about 60 direct reports and, by the Wall Street Journal's account, no belief in succession planning. He held 3.61% of the company, by Reuters's count. He did not control Nvidia by votes. He controlled it by being indispensable, and the board let a $4 trillion company depend on that. The governance discount was always there. The market had no reason to price it until this week.

One fact limits the China channel everyone expects: Nvidia's $108 billion guidance already assumes no data-centre compute revenue from China. The cost of this affair will be measured in trust, in Washington where the company needs licences and in boardrooms where it needs counterparties.

THE CHEAPER SHOVEL

Nvidia's gross margin was 75% last quarter. A leaderless Nvidia facing AMD, Broadcom and Google's in-house chips is a supplier with less power over customers whose combined capital budgets exceed $700 billion a year. If that power erodes, the loss falls on Nvidia's shareholders and the gain goes to the buyers of compute. One level up, the same thing is already happening to tokens. I am not forecasting where prices go. I am saying who benefits when they fall. A cheaper shovel is bad news for the shovel maker. It is not bad news for the mine. Some of the biggest beneficiaries of this cycle may be businesses that use AI rather than sell it.

NEXT WEEK'S EXAM

On Tuesday 17 November Nvidia reports its third quarter, the first without Huang. For years the division of labour on those calls was simple: the finance chief read the numbers and the founder sold the future. Now one person has to do both. Three answers matter more than the revenue line: whether guidance for the January quarter still rises, whether the guarantees and lab financings stand on the terms already signed, and whether the board gives a date for a permanent appointment.

Anthropic has set a range of $70 to $78 for 825 million shares, up to about $64 billion, with a further $26 billion of private investment alongside from Google, Nvidia and others, for a valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion, below what had been expected earlier in the year. Pricing is due on Wednesday 18 November and trading on Thursday 19 November. Axios reports annualised revenue of $81 billion in October and commitments of nearly $901 billion. Notice who is in the private placement: a supplier. Of the 825 million shares, about 801 million are new shares sold by the company: the money funds compute bills, not exits, which means the public is being asked to pay for the build-out before the return on it is known. SpaceX rose after its record June listing and then fell below its offer price within weeks. A strong first day will prove little. A pulled deal would prove a great deal, because it would narrow the equity window on which the financing chain now leans.

FOUR OBJECTIONS, ANSWERED

"This is the dot-com bubble again." The valuation is not: 14 times against more than 100. The utilisation is not: builders short of capacity against dark fibre. The financing might be, which is why I spend more time on debt than on demand.

"The demand is circular." At the margin, visibly. At the core, three cloud providers collected $110 billion in a quarter and more than half of Ramp's businesses pay for AI out of their own budgets. Circular financing inflates the pace. It did not invent the product.

"The Democrats will stop the data centres." No moratorium has been enacted. If one becomes law, that is a supply shock: it delays revenue, strands some of the capital raised this year and raises the value of capacity already built. It would hurt builders and chip volumes. It would not mean people stopped wanting the service.

"Adoption without profit is a fad." It may be an early stage. Only 37% see EBIT impact and that share did not move in a year: if it has not moved in another, I will worry. But customers who are not yet earning from AI are also paying less per unit of it, which is not how a fad ends. It is how a technology becomes ordinary.

WHO CAPTURES, WHO PAYS

AMD and Broadcom captured, on the day, part of the premium that left Nvidia. Hyperscalers capture bargaining power over their supplier. Users of AI capture the falling price of intelligence. A buyer of Nvidia at 14 times earnings captures a price that assumes the founder was the business.

The index holder pays: every pension and passive fund whose Nvidia holding is worth 30% less than five weeks ago, without anyone having taken a decision. Model developers pay if price competition outruns their commitments. Suppliers who built on a handshake pay if the handshake is renegotiated. Lenders pay if a developer cannot refinance. And gold settled on Thursday at a 52-week low of $3,889.40; by the Journal's account, investors are selling winners to cover losses in technology. When the hedge is sold to fund the losing trade, leverage is being unwound somewhere.

NO COLLAPSE DOES NOT MEAN NO COST

A repricing is not painless because it is not a collapse. About $1.75 trillion has left one stock in five weeks, and that stock sits in most index funds and pensions. Bowman's own warning ran through this channel: lower share prices weaken household spending and dearer credit hits housing and small business, with no need for a single data centre to be cancelled. Saying there is no collapse of AI is a statement about the technology and its users. It is not a promise about your portfolio.

WHAT WOULD PROVE ME WRONG

I would abandon the adoption thesis if, across several reporting periods, independent paying demand stagnated or reversed: Ramp's 56.8% falling, production use dropping when trials and subsidies end, a sustained inability to show net economic value. I would call it a crash of the whole system if two or more of the large builders cut 2027 capital plans for lack of demand rather than lack of chips or permits, if Nvidia's orders shrank rather than its multiple, or if the Anthropic listing failed and the debt market for data centres closed behind it. None of these has happened. Every one of them could.

WHAT I WOULD MONITOR

Nvidia on 17 November and Anthropic on 18 and 19 November. The succession, and whether the finance role is separated from the chief executive's. The 2027 capital-expenditure guides in late January, and the reason given for any change. Ramp's monthly index: paid adoption, token volume and token spend, read separately. Asset write-downs, capacity utilisation and customer concentration in the next filings. Spreads on AI-related debt. The first data-centre bills in Texas, Ohio and Georgia.

The criterion is measurable. If earnings estimates and paid adoption hold through those tests while multiples and token prices stay low, November 2026 was a repricing: painful, overdue in places, survivable. If they start to fall, I was wrong, and The Economist was early rather than late.

Markets have a useful habit of asking for evidence eventually. They also have a less useful habit of waiting until after the money has been spent.

If I were you, I would not confuse the fall of a man with the fall of a market, or the fall of a price with the fall of a business. A crash needs customers to leave. So far, only a chief executive has.

I do not expect the end of AI. I expect the end of the idea that an AI story is enough.

Roberto Balbino | Founder & CEO, Fintech SCB

🚆 TRAIN REVIEW: Special Express No. 43 (Bangkok to Ban Krut)

If you’re heading south from Bangkok for a few days by the sea, Special Express No. 43 is one train worth considering. It’s a daytime diesel railcar to Surat Thani, with stops at Hua Hin, Prachuap Khiri Khan, Ban Krut, Bang Saphan Yai and Chumphon. We took it as far as Ban Krut today. I’ll write about the trip itself later, but a few things are worth knowing about the train, especially if you’re counting on lunch!

We left Krung Thep Aphiwat at 07:30 and arrived at Ban Krut at 12:24. That’s just under five hours, and the fare was 392 baht.

💺 What’s it like on board?

There are three carriages. The seats are reversible, so everyone faces the direction of travel. Mine reclined and had a footrest, a fold-down table and a net pocket. Even when the passenger in front reclined, I still had enough legroom. There are curtains for the bright sunshine and hooks for a jacket or bag, though my jacket spent more time on me than on the hook. The carriage averaged about 20°C. Blankets are sometimes available if you ask.

A carry-on suitcase fits easily on the overhead rack. I saw a couple of cases up there that looked about 28 inches, though there’s also space for larger bags at the ends of the carriages. There are no power sockets at the seats, so bring a power bank if you’ll need to charge your phone.

Each carriage has two toilets, one of which may be a squat toilet. The ones I checked were clean and had toilet paper and a handheld bidet spray. Outside were washbasins, soap and a mirror.

🍜 Can you get food on board?

There’s no dining car, but shortly after we left Bangkok, the conductors came through taking orders for food from stations along the way. Everything was announced verbally in Thai, so if you don’t speak the language, it’s easy to miss your chance.

There were two rounds of orders. The first was for dry noodles from Ratchaburi (20 baht) and a Thai dessert from Phetchaburi (100 baht). Later, we were offered a choice of rice dishes for 50 baht each. These would come on board at Bang Saphan, just after our stop at Ban Krut. Too late for our lunch, but worth knowing if you’re staying on to Chumphon or Surat Thani.

The cleaner also came through offering bottled water, hot coffee, Ovaltine and Mama instant noodles for 10 to 30 baht. I’d still bring a packed meal, drinks and a few snacks. What you can get depends partly on where you get off.

🎟️ A few booking tips

From Bangkok, it’s 300 baht to Hua Hin or 392 baht to Ban Krut. Both journeys can be booked up to 30 days ahead. If you want to buy tickets further ahead for Ban Krut, booking through to Chumphon costs just 37 baht more and gives you a 90-day booking window. You can still get off at Ban Krut.

Tomorrow we’re catching No. 43 again from Ban Krut to Chumphon. For a short hop like this, tickets only go on sale one day ahead. We bought ours at Krung Thep Aphiwat this morning, though we could have booked online from midnight last night. For Sunday night’s sleeper back to Bangkok, we booked from Surat Thani to get the longer booking window and plan to join the train at Chumphon. More about that later. 

Would I take No. 43 again? For Ban Krut, I like being there by lunchtime. If you’d rather save money, Ordinary No. 255 is a lot cheaper and gets in about two hours later. It also goes on to Chumphon, so that was our backup for tomorrow if No. 43 had been full.

🚆 Have you taken Special Express No. 43? How was your journey, and what’s one tip you’d give someone taking it for the first time?

According to court documents, Rambhai and his co-conspirators set up and carried out staged armed robberies at convenience stores and fast-food restaurants across a few states. All of this was done in front of security cameras, so when the victims called the police, they could offer their help and qualify for a U-visa. The guards would then bend the inmate in half, and sometimes stomp on the device, which resulted in serious injury, including broken spines. After his tenure at Adra Prison, Alsheikh briefly served as Governor of Deir Es-Zour, a critical oil-rich region on the Syria-Iraq border, and where he was also accused of brutal crackdowns on dissidents.

It is believed that Alsheikh entered the United States and settled in Los Angeles, California at some point in 2020. Shortly after, he applied for U.S. citizenship. In 2022, the Syrian Emergency Task Force alerted the United States that Alsheikh was in the country, and in July 2024, a complaint was filed that Alsheikh lied on his visa and citizenship applications about having never persecuted any person on any basis and having never been involved in killing or trying to kill someone. He was then taken into custody. After a two-week federal jury trial, he was convicted and is now awaiting sentencing. 
(OPA, March 2026; Courthouse News Service, March 2026; PBS, March 2026)
Christopher Leon Bailey (March 16, 2026)
On March 16, ICE agents arrested Jamaican national Christopher Leon Bailey in connection with a January road rage incident that took place in Ridley Township, Pennsylvania. On January 23, Bailey was arrested by local police after he allegedly pulled a knife on and attempted to stab an individual following a near collision. He then returned to his vehicle to chase down and run over the victim. ICE reported that Bailey had overstayed his tourist visa in 2009, and he was previously arrested by ICE in Philadelphia in 2023 for violating immigration laws. Nvidia lost its chief executive days before earnings while the industry committed capital it has not earned yet.

NVIDIA · RESIGNATION EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY
Nvidia said November 12 that Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. The board accepted the resignation November 11, per its Form 8-K. CFO Colette Kress is interim chief and keeps the finance role, and director Harvey C. Jones became the board's first chair. Shares closed down 4.34% at $166.19, with third-quarter results scheduled November 17.

ANTHROPIC · 6X THE SHARES ON OFFER
Anthropic's IPO drew about six times the orders for the shares available, Bloomberg reported November 12. The company and selling shareholders offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78, for up to $64.4 billion. A $26 billion placement goes to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. Anthropic lists pricing November 18 and Nasdaq trading November 19 under ANT.

SPACEX · MORE THAN $74B
SpaceX said November 12 it plans more than $74 billion for two AI campuses: over $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, and about $50 billion in Cochise County, Arizona. The Arizona campus draws up to 6 gigawatts across nine buildings. Both need local approval December 9, and a 2,400-signature petition asks the county to deny the permit.

NEBIUS · $40-45B GUIDED FOR 2027
Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% on the year, then cut 2026 revenue guidance to $3.0-3.2 billion on third-party capacity delays. It raised 2026 capital spending to about $27 billion and guided 2027 spending at $40-45 billion, against a $28.77 billion estimate. The company says 75% to 85% of 2027 spending is covered by customer prepayments and asset-backed financing. Shares fell 16%.

GOOGLE · $1.50 PER MILLION TOKENS
Google introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen November 12, a fast tier for coding and agentic work. It costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens across a 1-million-token window, with a free tier. Google puts it at 51 on the Artificial Analysis index by default, 54 at maximum, against 50 for Argon. Hydrogen becomes the default in AI Mode.

THE THROUGH-LINE
A leadership vacuum opened at the firm anchoring AI supply days before it reports; the rest of the industry spent against future revenue. Supplier equity sits beside the Anthropic listing, prepayments cover Nebius, and SpaceX campuses await permits. The buildout is being financed from outside the builders' balance sheets.

text:
Sonia Gandhi: A Life of Love, Dignity, Courage and Service

THE "BELONGING": A PERSONAL JOURNEY, A NATIONAL STORY

Smt. Sonia Gandhi’s " Belonging: A Journey of Love" - is more than a political memoir. It recounts a journey from Italy to India, shaped by love, loss, service, a deep sense of belonging to this country and lasting devotion to its people.

I have always been a great admirer of Madam Gandhi. I first met Rajiv ji and Sonia ji while serving at Rashtrapati Bhavan as an Indian Air Force fighter pilot deputed to the office of the President of India. 

As I entered public life, she placed her trust in me. She gave me the opportunity to serve as a minister and later as president of the Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee. I have served six terms as MLA, represented our people in Parliament and held ministerial responsibilities in undivided Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

When I look back at my political journey, I do so with gratitude: I owe everything I have achieved in public life to her faith in me. That bond makes reading "Belonging" meaningful. The book traces Sonia Gandhi’s life from her childhood in Italy and her meeting with Rajiv Gandhi in Cambridge to her arrival in India and the making of a home here.

Its pages place the private story of a wife and mother alongside the history of a nation. The deaths of Sanjay Gandhi, Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi were not only defining public events; they were devastating losses within a family. The memoir brings that human dimension into view.

I have watched Madam Gandhi withstand personal attacks that too often descended into unfairness and prejudice. Through every phase, she has remained an example of grace, dignity and decency. The restraint and composure with which she has met hostility say much about her character.
In public life, where it is easy to answer insults with anger, she has consistently shown self-command and a profound sense of responsibility.
Her decision to enter politics after years of reluctance was an act of duty.

As Congress president, she gave the party direction and renewed purpose through difficult years. Her leadership helped bring together a broad coalition, and her decision to decline the office of Prime Minister in 2004, while supporting Dr. Manmohan Singh as Prime Minister, remains an extraordinary moment of political judgment and personal conviction.

The title captures the book’s deepest theme. "Belonging" is not determined by birthplace alone; it grows through love, shared struggle and service. Sonia Gandhi made India her home, and devoted herself to its people and democratic life. Her memoir offers a rare opportunity to understand the woman behind the public role: a person shaped by affection, bereavement, courage and commitment.

For me, this book is also a reminder of a debt of gratitude. Madam Gandhi’s confidence gave me opportunities that shaped my life in the Congress and in public service. I remain profoundly thankful.

"Belonging" is a moving account of personal endurance and public duty, and a tribute to a leader whose grace under pressure has earned the admiration of countless people, including me.

N. Uttam Kumar Reddy, 
Telangana Minister for Irrigation and Civil Supplies. 

Former Indian Air Force fighter pilot.
