text:
Daniel, Yes, over the years, I have seen polls indicating that a slight majority of Canadians want fewer immigrants. In 2022, as high as 58% said there were too many immigrants arriving in Canada. 

These are “soft” numbers, however. In 2026, the same poll company, Environics, found that this number had dropped to 48%, as Canadians were raising their elbows in a state of national pride for Canada’s multiethnic identity.

The main reasons Canadians want lower immigrants are economic or social, pointing to lack of housing, crowded hospitals or schools. They are not racially motivated. 

Yes, a Léger poll in 2024 found that 48% want mass deportation of illegals who commit serious crimes. 

The government has no problem dealing with this issue: Carney deported a record 26, 000  + “inadmissible” migrants in 2025. Now he is importing more legal immigrants than ever with very high approval ratings. 

There is a world of difference between this and calling for deportation of millions of nonwhite citizens. 

Yes, you can advocate for remigration of citizens. But the penalties are high; you can be easily fired, and it is very difficult to function professionally or obtain a career. This is one reason so many in our side are anons advocating and inhabiting online bubbles.

What I am saying here is not “counter signalling”. It is analysis of the political realities of white identity politics. I have been advocating “ far right” ideas concerning immigration issues for about  14 years. 

The best thing about organizations like DS is they offer a social network for white identity politics. It is great to get together, exchange thoughts and feelings, and plan courses of action. 

The notion that one can deport millions of Canadian nonwhite citizens is, I am sorry, delusional. (I do believe, however, that remigration should be advocated by the AfD). It goes directly against the Charter; and it is morally unacceptable to the vast majority of Canadians. 

What we need is an organization that advocates for white Canadians within the inescapable legal reality of liberal multiculturalism. A lot can be achieved from this simple strategy.

text:
A year or so ago, Xiao Li was seeing floods of Nvidia chip deals on WeChat. A real estate contractor turned data center project manager, he had pivoted to AI infrastructure in 2023, drawn by the promise of China’s AI craze. 

At that time, traders in his circle bragged about securing shipments of high-performing Nvidia GPUs that were subject to US export restrictions. Many were smuggled through overseas channels to Shenzhen. At the height of the demand, a single Nvidia H100 chip, a kind that is essential to training AI models, could sell for up to 200,000 yuan ($28,000) on the black market. 

Now, his WeChat feed and industry group chats tell a different story. Traders are more discreet in their dealings, and prices have come back down to earth. Meanwhile, two data center projects Li is familiar with are struggling to secure further funding from investors who anticipate poor returns, forcing project leads to sell off surplus GPUs. “It seems like everyone is selling, but few are buying,” he says.

Just months ago, a boom in data center construction was at its height, fueled by both government and private investors. However, many newly built facilities are now sitting empty. According to people on the ground who spoke to MIT Technology Review—including contractors, an executive at a GPU server company, and project managers—most of the companies running these data centers are struggling to stay afloat. The local Chinese outlets Jiazi Guangnian and 36Kr report that up to 80% of China’s newly built computing resources remain unused.

Renting out GPUs to companies that need them for training AI models—the main business model for the new wave of data centers—was once seen as a sure bet. But with the rise of DeepSeek and a sudden change in the economics around AI, the industry is faltering.

“The growing pain China’s AI industry is going through is largely a result of inexperienced players—corporations and local governments—jumping on the hype train, building facilities that aren’t optimal for today’s need,” says Jimmy Goodrich, senior advisor for technology to the RAND Corporation. 

The upshot is that projects are failing, energy is being wasted, and data centers have become “distressed assets” whose investors are keen to unload them at below-market rates. The situation may eventually prompt government intervention, he says: “The Chinese government is likely to step in, take over, and hand them off to more capable operators.”

A chaotic building boom

When ChatGPT exploded onto the scene in late 2022, the response in China was swift. The central government designated AI infrastructure as a national priority, urging local governments to accelerate the development of so-called smart computing centers—a term coined to describe AI-focused data centers.

In 2023 and 2024, over 500 new data center projects were announced everywhere from Inner Mongolia to Guangdong, according to KZ Consulting, a market research firm. According to the China Communications Industry Association Data Center Committee, a state-affiliated industry association, at least 150 of the newly built data centers were finished and running by the end of 2024. State-owned enterprises, publicly traded firms, and state-affiliated funds lined up to invest in them, hoping to position themselves as AI front-runners. Local governments heavily promoted them in the hope they’d stimulate the economy and establish their region as a key AI hub. 

However, as these costly construction projects continue, the Chinese frenzy over large language models is losing momentum. In 2024 alone, over 144 companies registered with the Cyberspace Administration of China—the country’s central internet regulator—to develop their own LLMs. Yet according to the Economic Observer, a Chinese publication, only about 10% of those companies were still actively investing in large-scale model training by the end of the year.

China’s political system is highly centralized, with local government officials typically moving up the ranks through regional appointments. As a result, many local leaders prioritize short-term economic projects that demonstrate quick results—often to gain favor with higher-ups—rather than long-term development. Large, high-profile infrastructure projects have long been a tool for local officials to boost their political careers.

The post-pandemic economic downturn only intensified this dynamic. With China’s real estate sector—once the backbone of local economies—slumping for the first time in decades, officials scrambled to find alternative growth drivers. In the meantime, the country’s once high-flying internet industry was also entering a period of stagnation. In this vacuum, AI infrastructure became the new stimulus of choice.

“AI felt like a shot of adrenaline,” says Li. “A lot of money that used to flow into real estate is now going into AI data centers.”

By 2023, major corporations—many of them with little prior experience in AI—began partnering with local governments to capitalize on the trend. Some saw AI infrastructure as a way to justify business expansion or boost stock prices, says Fang Cunbao, a data center project manager based in Beijing. Among them were companies like Lotus, an MSG manufacturer, and Jinlun Technology, a textile firm—hardly the names one would associate with cutting-edge AI technology.

This gold-rush approach meant that the push to build AI data centers was largely driven from the top down, often with little regard for actual demand or technical feasibility, say Fang, Li, and multiple on-the-ground sources, who asked to speak anonymously for fear of political repercussions. Many projects were led by executives and investors with limited expertise in AI infrastructure, they say. In the rush to keep up, many were constructed hastily and fell short of industry standards. 

“Putting all these large clusters of chips together is a very difficult exercise, and there are very few companies or individuals who know how to do it at scale,” says Goodrich. “This is all really state-of-the-art computer engineering. I’d be surprised if most of these smaller players know how to do it. A lot of the freshly built data centers are quickly strung together and don’t offer the stability that a company like DeepSeek would want.”

To make matters worse, project leaders often relied on middlemen and brokers—some of whom exaggerated demand forecasts or manipulated procurement processes to pocket government subsidies, sources say. 

By the end of 2024, the excitement that once surrounded China’s data center boom was  curdling into disappointment. The reason is simple: GPU rental is no longer a particularly  lucrative business.

The DeepSeek reckoning

The business model of data centers is in theory straightforward: They make money by renting out GPU clusters to companies that need computing capacity for AI training. In reality, however, securing clients is proving difficult. Only a few top tech companies in China are now drawing heavily on computing power to train their AI models. Many smaller players have been giving up on pretraining their models or otherwise shifting their strategy since the rise of DeepSeek, which broke the internet with R1, its open-source reasoning model that matches the performance of ChatGPT o1 but was built at a fraction of its cost. 

“DeepSeek is a moment of reckoning for the Chinese AI industry. The burning question shifted from ‘Who can make the best large language model?’ to ‘Who can use them better?’” says Hancheng Cao, an assistant professor of information systems at Emory University. 

The rise of reasoning models like DeepSeek’s R1 and OpenAI’s ChatGPT o1 and o3 has also changed what businesses want from a data center. With this technology, most of the computing needs come from conducting step-by-step logical deductions in response to users’ queries, not from the process of training and creating the model in the first place. This reasoning process often yields better results but takes significantly more time. As a result, hardware with low latency (the time it takes for data to pass from one point on a network to another) is paramount. Data centers need to be located near major tech hubs to minimize transmission delays and ensure access to highly skilled operations and maintenance staff. 

This change means many data centers built in central, western, and rural China—where electricity and land are cheaper—are losing their allure to AI companies. In Zhengzhou, a city in Li’s home province of Henan, a newly built data center is even distributing free computing vouchers to local tech firms but still struggles to attract clients. 

Additionally, a lot of the new data centers that have sprung up in recent years were optimized for pretraining workloads—large, sustained computations run on massive data sets—rather than for inference, the process of running trained reasoning models to respond to user inputs in real time. Inference-friendly hardware differs from what’s traditionally used for large-scale AI training. 

GPUs like Nvidia H100 and A100 are designed for massive data processing, prioritizing speed and memory capacity. But as AI moves toward real-time reasoning, the industry seeks chips that are more efficient, responsive, and cost-effective. Even a minor miscalculation in infrastructure needs can render a data center suboptimal for the tasks clients require.

In these circumstances, the GPU rental price has dropped to an all-time low. A recent report from the Chinese media outlet Zhineng Yongxian said that an Nvidia H100 server configured with eight GPUs now rents for 75,000 yuan per month, down from highs of around 180,000. Some data centers would rather leave their facilities sitting empty than run the risk of losing even more money because they are so costly to run, says Fan: “The revenue from having a tiny part of the data center running simply wouldn’t cover the electricity and maintenance cost.”

“It’s paradoxical—China faces the highest acquisition costs for Nvidia chips, yet GPU leasing prices are extraordinarily low,” Li says. There’s an oversupply of computational power, especially in central and west China, but at the same time, there’s a shortage of cutting-edge chips. 

However, not all brokers were looking to make money from data centers in the first place. Instead, many were interested in gaming government benefits all along. Some operators exploit the sector for subsidized green electricity, obtaining permits to generate and sell power, according to Fang and some Chinese media reports. Instead of using the energy for AI workloads, they resell it back to the grid at a premium. In other cases, companies acquire land for data center development to qualify for state-backed loans and credits, leaving facilities unused while still benefiting from state funding, according to the local media outlet Jiazi Guangnian.

“Towards the end of 2024, no clear-headed contractor and broker in the market would still go into the business expecting direct profitability,” says Fang. “Everyone I met is leveraging the data center deal for something else the government could offer.”

A necessary evil

Despite the underutilization of data centers, China’s central government is still throwing its weight behind a push for AI infrastructure. In early 2025, it convened an AI industry symposium, emphasizing the importance of self-reliance in this technology. 

Major Chinese tech companies are taking note, making investments aligning with this national priority. Alibaba Group announced plans to invest over $50 billion in cloud computing and AI hardware infrastructure over the next three years, while ByteDance plans to invest around $20 billion in GPUs and data centers.

In the meantime, companies in the US are doing likewise. Major tech firms including OpenAI, Softbank, and Oracle have teamed up to commit to the Stargate initiative, which plans to invest up to $500 billion over the next four years to build advanced data centers and computing infrastructure. ​Given the AI competition between the two countries, experts say that China is unlikely to scale back its efforts. “If generative AI is going to be the killer technology, infrastructure is going to be the determinant of success,”  says Goodrich, the tech policy advisor to RAND.

“The Chinese central government will likely see [underused data centers] as a necessary evil to develop an important capability, a growing pain of sorts. You have the failed projects and distressed assets, and the state will consolidate and clean it up. They see the end, not the means,” Goodrich says.

Demand remains strong for Nvidia chips, and especially the H20 chip, which was custom-designed for the Chinese market. One industry source, who requested not to be identified under his company policy, confirmed that the H20, a lighter, faster model optimized for AI inference, is currently the most popular Nvidia chip, followed by the H100, which continues to flow steadily into China even though sales are officially restricted by US sanctions. Some of the new demand is driven by companies deploying their own versions of DeepSeek’s open-source models.

For now, many data centers in China sit in limbo—built for a future that has yet to arrive. Whether they will find a second life remains uncertain. For Fang Cunbao, DeepSeek’s success has become a moment of reckoning, casting doubt on the assumption that an endless expansion of AI infrastructure guarantees progress.

That’s just a myth, he now realizes. At the start of this year, Fang decided to quit the data center industry altogether. “The market is too chaotic. The early adopters profited, but now it’s just people chasing policy loopholes,” he says. He’s decided to go into AI education next. 

“What stands between now and a future where AI is actually everywhere,” he says, “is not infrastructure anymore, but solid plans to deploy the technology.”

text:
Before his ouster, Nvidia ($NVDA) founder Jensen Huang reportedly belittled incoming CEO Colette Kress during an August clash over AI financing, calling her "a deer in the headlights" and a "reporting CFO" incapable of shaping strategy or making decisions, The Wall Street Journal reports.

* Internal Clash: Kress questioned deal selection, guarantee valuations and returns as Huang grew concerned about billions in financial exposure to AI customers unable to afford Nvidia chips.
* Family Involvement: Huang's son-in-law Nico Caprez, promoted to VP in January, and executive Raj Mirpuri offered cloud providers credit guarantees, sometimes promising deals within weeks. Nvidia sought a share of customer revenue in exchange for guarantees designed to lower borrowing costs. Kress reportedly tried to rein in Caprez.
* OpenAI Deal: Nvidia considered a $250B backstop for an Ohio data center OpenAI planned to lease and equip with roughly $300B in Nvidia chips. After the proposal surfaced in July, shares fell 5%, erasing $250B in market value. Kress halved Nvidia's initial commitment before a smaller deal was signed August 17.
* Financing Pullback: Nvidia later paused some deals, adding executive and board reviews that slowed approvals. Kress publicly defended the investments, disputing circular-financing concerns and predicting excellent returns.
* Competitive Pressure: Huang warned major cloud customers were developing alternative chips to reduce Nvidia dependence, while enormous wafer and memory purchase commitments approached like an "avalanche."
* Valuation Concerns: Huang privately expressed frustration as Nvidia's average monthly valuation multiple fell from 23 in May to 16 in October. Nvidia responded partly with a record stock buyback.
* October Strategy Shift: Huang urged cloud CEOs to preserve chip pricing and customer diversity, citing a Japanese soup vendor who refused to sell all his inventory to a few buyers. "You are not establishing the value of my products," he warned.

A trade and investment delegation from St. Louis, Missouri, led by Mayor Cara Spencer, is visiting Kenya to deepen Kenya–United States commercial relations and unlock new opportunities for exporters, businesses and investors.

As part of the visit,a High-Level Trade and Investment Roundtable was held in Nairobi, jointly convened by the Embassy of Kenya in Washington, D.C., the U.S. Embassy in Nairobi and AMCHAM Kenya bringing together government representatives, business leaders and institutions to explore partnerships that promote trade, strengthen local production and create jobs.

The engagement underscores Kenya’s commitment to expanding commercial diplomacy beyond national capitals by building direct connections with American cities, states and business communities.

In remarks delivered on her behalf by Deputy Director for International Trade, Robert Ng’ong’a, Principal Secretary for Trade Regina Ombam outlined key priority areas for collaboration, including agriculture and agro-processing; healthcare, pharmaceuticals and biosciences; ICT and digital services; manufacturing and infrastructure; as well as tourism, education and cultural exchange.

The State Department for Foreign Affairs was represented by Mr. Evans Maturo, Deputy Director General for Economic and Commercial Affairs, while the State Department for Agriculture was represented by the Agriculture Secretary, Mr. James Wanjohi.

Kenya is keen to strengthen linkages between local exporters and American buyers, with significant opportunities in specialty coffee, value-added tea, macadamia nuts, processed foods, apparel and textiles, leather products, flowers and eligible horticultural products. The focus is on increasing both the volume and diversity of Kenyan exports to the U.S. market while creating new opportunities for local enterprises.

The mission was coordinated by Mr. Geoffrey Odero, Commercial Attaché at the Embassy of Kenya in Washington, D.C., who facilitated strategic engagements and connected the visiting delegation with key government and private-sector partners.

With its strategic location, skilled workforce and growing digital economy, Kenya offers an attractive investment destination and a gateway to the wider regional and continental markets through the East African Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area.

To translate the discussions into tangible outcomes, Kenya has proposed the establishment of a Kenya–St. Louis Commercial Cooperation Framework bringing together the State Department for Trade, Nairobi City County and World Trade Center St. Louis. The proposed framework will provide a platform for coordinated follow-up on identified business opportunities and strengthen institutional and business linkages beyond the visit.

Or maybe you’d call it a "cold" attitude?

She treated me a bit coldly.

That’s why I, Babidi-sama, dislike this girl who gave me the cold shoulder.

Also, her face isn’t really my type—that’s probably a factor, too.

For the record, she happens to be tall and has a good build—which is my type—but I’ve convinced myself that the girls I actually like are supposed to be "cute."

Though, to be honest, I can’t quite recall exactly what her face looks like.

Anyway—phew, that took a while.

So, here’s the issue I wanted advice on.

One day, this girl—the one I’ve taken an interest in—said something to me.

At the checkout counter, of course.

"Would you like to sign up for a Lawson card?"

I, Babidi-sama, never sign up for these kinds of loyalty cards.

I don’t want my personal information leaking out.

But, since it was a suggestion from this girl I’m interested in...

...I went ahead and said yes.

And then, I started to wonder:

"Why did she ask me if I wanted to sign up for a card?"

I actually asked this on one of those online forums for relationship advice.

The response was brutal.

"You’re a regular customer—of course she’s going to suggest it, isn't she?"

Well, I suppose that’s true.

But for me—Babidi-sama—it’s not that simple.

I just couldn't be sure.

I ended up reading nothing but harsh comments.

You know, the kind that are just pure criticism?

It left me, Babidi-sama, completely traumatized.

I mean, surely no one else is as big an idiot as me to ask about something like this, right?

But isn't it obvious?

She touched my hand, didn't she?

I mentioned that earlier, didn't I?

You wouldn't touch the hand of a customer you dislike, would you?

I mean, you wouldn't—right?

That’s exactly why I, Babidi-sama, was asking for advice in the first place!

Otherwise, since I’m a regular, it would make sense for her to suggest it, wouldn't it?

Maybe I should talk about this now. How things ended with this girl.

But first—there’s that machine at Lawson, the Loppi, right?

The terminal where you can buy movie tickets.

Even though Babidi-sama could have operated it himself, he deliberately asked this girl how to use it.

Finding ways to create a connection like that—that’s just "Babidi-sama’s style."

What was the movie ticket for, again?

It was a Will Smith movie, wasn't it?

Just now, Babidi-sama said to me:

"If you mention Will Smith’s name here, you’re going to get sued."

I mean, he’s a Hollywood star—there’s no way I’d get sued for that, right?

"Explain why you wouldn't get sued," Babidi-sama demanded.

Well, obviously, no one’s going to sue over something like this.

The movie where Will Smith starred alongside his son...

I can’t recall the title right now.

I’ll write it down once I remember.

The Pursuit of Happyness—

was that it?

Anyway, let’s talk about how it ended.

It was around New Year’s, I think.

Babidi-sama decided to do something...

Something that would never even cross anyone else’s mind.

You probably wouldn't guess it—it’s just so bizarre.

He went and bought—of all things—New Year’s greeting postcards.

And he actually tried to write something on them and send them off.

Why didn't he just ask for her contact information like a normal person?

He’s perfectly capable of talking, isn't he?

They were on speaking terms by then, surely.

So, why not just ask?

Honestly, he really should stop with these creepy tactics.

Babidi-sama drove to the Lawson—it was in the morning, I believe.

He’d happened to find out that she worked an early-morning shift—a time when there wouldn't be any other customers around.

That’s the early morning for you.

text:
FRIDAY MORNING DISPATCH UPDATE

November 13, 2026 | Denver Metro and Front Range

Police, fire and emergency crews responded to numerous incidents overnight and into Friday morning, including multiple highway crashes, reported assaults, weapons calls, domestic disturbances, vehicle fires and transit disruptions.

The following incidents are listed from newest to oldest, based on dispatch timestamps. Times are Mountain Standard Time.

FRIDAY MORNING | NOVEMBER 13

8:08 AM | Scooter Blocks RTD Train

East 40th Avenue, Denver

An eastbound RTD train was forced into an emergency stop after a scooter or bicycle was left dangerously close to the tracks. The train reportedly slowed to approximately 2 mph before stopping. Personnel were requested to remove the obstruction so subsequent trains could proceed.

8:04 AM | Child Possibly Injured in Two-Vehicle Crash

Huron Street and Thornton Parkway, Thornton

Emergency crews responded to a two-vehicle collision in the southbound lanes of Huron Street, north of Thornton Parkway, near a vacant gas station. An 11-year-old reportedly suffered a possible shoulder injury. Engine 72 was investigating.

8:01 AM | Vehicle Strikes Pedestrian Near High School

South Picadilly Street, Aurora

Fire and medical personnel were dispatched to a reported collision involving a vehicle and pedestrian near Crest High School. The pedestrian’s condition was not immediately available.

7:59 AM | Fire Reported Along Westbound Sixth Avenue

Sixth Avenue near Kipling Street

Dispatch traffic indicated a possible fire along westbound Sixth Avenue near Kipling, with traffic backing up in the area. The cause and extent of the fire were not immediately confirmed.

7:49 AM | Purse Stolen During Vehicle Break-In

North Highway 287, Lafayette

Police responded to a fitness center after someone reportedly smashed a vehicle window and stole a purse. Officers were investigating the theft.

7:42 AM | Reported Drug Activity

Broadway and Speer Boulevard, Denver

Officers were dispatched after a report of approximately seven people possibly using narcotics near southbound Broadway and Speer. An additional unit was assigned to provide cover.

7:41 AM | Vehicle Fire Reported Extinguished

Westbound highway shoulder near mile marker 246

Transportation radio traffic indicated a vehicle fire on the westbound shoulder had been extinguished. No traffic blockage was reported.

7:37 AM | Water Flowing From Manhole

West Cannon Place and Sutton Circle, Lafayette

Public Works was notified of water continuing to flow from a manhole near Cannon Place and Sutton Circle. Water was reportedly running down the street.

7:33 AM | Dead Turkey Creates Traffic Hazard

South Havana Street and East First Avenue, Aurora

Public Works received a report of a dead turkey in the roadway, creating a possible traffic hazard. Police notification was discussed.

7:30 AM | SUV Blocking Bus Stop

Wadsworth Bypass

A white Ford SUV was reported parked at a bus stop since the previous day, potentially obstructing access for transit passengers.

7:18 AM | Three-Vehicle Crash

20th Street, Denver

A three-vehicle collision left one vehicle disabled. Crews moved vehicles to the left shoulder and spread sand. No injuries were subsequently reported.

7:08 AM | Welfare Check at Union Station

Union Station, Denver

Transit officers were sent to check on two people appearing to be sleeping or slouched over near an elevator. Surveillance cameras reportedly showed both individuals, and one was said to have a lighter. A cover unit assisted.

7:05 AM | Three-Vehicle Crash Blocks Lane

Westbound I-76 near East 88th Avenue, Commerce City

Colorado State Patrol requested fire and medical assistance after a three-vehicle collision. One lane was blocked. Responders reported minor vehicle damage and that all occupants were outside their vehicles.

7:02 AM | Update on I-70 Vehicle Fire

Westbound I-70 near mile marker 255, Golden

A vehicle involved in an earlier fire was reported on the shoulder, with all travel lanes reopened. Colorado State Patrol continued providing traffic protection.

7:00 AM | Three Vehicles Blocking I-76

Westbound I-76 east of US-85

Three vehicles were reported blocking the left lane. A responding unit requested to turn around and return to the scene. This may relate to the collision reported minutes later near 88th Avenue.

6:53 AM | Trespassing Report Behind Car Wash

Cannon Circle, Louisville

Officers responded to a wooded area behind a car wash following a trespassing complaint. The incident was subsequently reported Code 4, indicating the situation appeared resolved.

6:49 AM | Semi and Truck Collision, One Hospitalized

Airport Boulevard on-ramp, Aurora

A semi and another truck collided on an Airport Boulevard on-ramp. Damage was described as minor, but one person was transported to University Hospital.

6:43 AM | Reported Knife Assault

Green Valley Ranch Boulevard, Aurora

Police and emergency medical personnel responded to a possible knife-related assault. An injured man was reported down the street while a thin adult male suspect reportedly fled the area. The circumstances and extent of injuries remained unclear.

6:43 AM | Fire Alarm at Littleton Police Department

West Berry Avenue, Littleton

South Metro Fire Rescue dispatched Engine 11 to a commercial fire alarm at the Littleton Police Department. No confirmed fire was reported in the available dispatch summary.

6:41 AM | Assault With Injuries

East Exposition Avenue near South Ironton Street, Denver

Emergency crews were dispatched to an apartment following a report of an assault with injuries. Additional information about the victim was not available.

6:36 AM | Assault Victim Requires Medical Assistance

Commerce City, East Street area

Police requested fire and medical assistance for a possible assault victim. Police were already on scene, and the medical response was requested as routine.

6:29 AM | Gun Discovered Under Bed

Lydia Drive, Lafayette

Police responded after a firearm was discovered beneath a bed inside a residence. The reporting party believed the gun belonged to their father and had not been removed from a safe box.

6:28 AM | Road Rage Involving Red Truck

Niwot Road and 107th Street, Boulder County

A driver reported that a red truck attempted to force their vehicle off the roadway while traveling southbound. The truck’s driver was reportedly yelling and swearing. The reporting party was following the vehicle and willing to provide a statement.

6:04 AM | Truck and Grass Fire Closes I-70 Lanes

Westbound I-70 near mile marker 255, Golden

Fire crews responded to a truck pulling a trailer that was fully involved in flames. Fire was reported in the cab and hood, and nearby grass also caught fire.

Lanes two and three were closed while firefighters worked to contain the blaze. A later update indicated the vehicle was on the shoulder and all lanes had reopened.

6:02 AM | Two-Vehicle Crash

East 88th Avenue and Tower Road, Commerce City

A dark SUV and black Toyota Tacoma collided. One person reported neck pain. Both vehicles were off the roadway with minor to moderate damage.

A separate medical call in the dispatch traffic concerned a 46-year-old man with a worsening spider bite on Oneida Street.

5:40 AM | Trespassing Complaint at Dollar Tree

West 84th Avenue, Federal Heights

Deputies were dispatched after an unwanted person was reportedly sleeping outside a Dollar Tree and refused requests to leave. Broken glass was also reported nearby.

5:10 AM | Driver Reports Being Followed

West Colfax Avenue and Brentwood Street, Lakewood

Police responded after a caller reported a vehicle repeatedly honking, flashing its lights and following them.

4:59 AM | Hit-and-Run Involving Two SUVs

Interstate 25

A white Toyota RAV4 and gray Mazda SUV were reportedly involved in a hit-and-run collision. One vehicle continued driving, and a callback was requested.

4:58 AM | Possible RTD Bus Collision

C-470 interchange

Transportation personnel received a report involving a possibly disabled RTD bus and another vehicle. The bus was reportedly attempting to cross multiple traffic lanes, prompting a request for someone to investigate.

4:53 AM | Assault at Old Town Arvada Parking Garage

Vance Street, Arvada

A man reported being assaulted by an unknown person wearing orange near the bicycle area of the Old Town Arvada parking garage. Security requested additional police units.

4:43 AM | Roadway Burn Damage

Mile marker 259, reported East Colfax area

Transportation radio traffic described possible burn marks in the asphalt and a roadway hazard. Another unit was requested. The exact roadway location requires confirmation.

4:28 AM | Reckless Driver Without Headlights

Westbound I-70 near mile marker 259, Golden

A Nissan Murano was reported traveling without headlights or taillights while drifting between lanes. The reporting driver maintained visual contact and offered to provide a written statement.

4:08 AM | Missing At-Risk Juvenile

East 10th Avenue area, Denver

Denver police issued a request for assistance locating a missing juvenile who had not returned home from school. Dispatch information indicated the child has intellectual disabilities and may use public transportation. The child’s whereabouts were not established in the available report.

3:56 AM | Bus Crash

Westgate and 43rd Avenue area, Denver

A bus collision was reported near 43rd Street. No passengers were reportedly aboard at the time.

3:27 AM | Woman Reportedly Pulled Into Apartment

West 10th Avenue, Lakewood

Police responded after a witness reported hearing a woman yelling for help and seeing a man pull her back into an apartment. No weapons were reported. The woman’s condition was not available.

3:26 AM | Traffic Stop

1600 Block of Pierce Street, Lakewood

Police conducted a traffic stop involving a vehicle with two occupants. Dispatch indicated the vehicle was briefly lost and another unit was requested.

3:01 AM | Police Search for Armed Shooting Suspect

South Federal Circle, Littleton

Police issued information about a suspect sought in connection with a reported shooting near South Federal Circle around 1:09 AM.

The person was believed to be armed and associated with a white sedan displaying temporary registration tags. Officers were instructed to contact Littleton police if the suspect was located.

2:43 AM | Armed Suspect Bulletin

400 Block of South Federal Circle, Littleton

An earlier dispatch described a woman believed to have a firearm and possibly leaving in a white sedan. This appears related to the subsequent shooting suspect bulletin. The two dispatch summaries contain differing time and vehicle details.

2:32 AM | Pickup Strikes Railroad Crossing Barrier

East 40th Avenue and York Street, Denver

A white pickup reportedly struck a median and railroad crossing arm. Officers were checking the scene and reviewing camera footage.

2:20 AM | Man Seriously Injured in Possible Assault

North Iola Street and East 17th Avenue, Aurora

Emergency crews responded to a 52-year-old man who was conscious and breathing but reportedly vomiting, unable to stand and having difficulty seeing.

Dispatch information suggested he may have been struck in the head and subsequently hit his head on the floor. There was also an unclear reference to a knife.

2:17 AM | Wrong-Way Driver on Highway 6

Highway 6 near Wadsworth Boulevard, Lakewood

A gray SUV was reportedly traveling the wrong direction at approximately 40 mph. Police and transportation officials were notified.

2:04 AM | Assault at Apartment

West 58th Avenue, Arvada

Medic 52 was dispatched to a reported assault at an apartment in the West 58th Avenue area. Responders were instructed to stage nearby.

2:02 AM | Repeated Noise Complaint

South Teller Street, Lakewood

Officers responded after a caller complained about an upstairs neighbor making loud noises resembling objects being dropped. Dispatch referenced previous disturbances at the location, including a possible firearms-related incident.

2:00 AM | Juvenile Reportedly Took Pills

East Mississippi Avenue area, Aurora

Emergency crews were dispatched after a report that a juvenile male had taken pills in a park. Responders were directed to the north side of the park. The dispatch headline described him as conscious.

1:58 AM | Possible Overdose at Aurora City Park

9701 East 16th Avenue, Aurora

Fire and police responded to a possible overdose at Aurora City Park near Dayton Street. The patient’s condition was not immediately available.

1:38 AM | Two Assault Reports

Motel 6, 9920 West 49th Avenue, Wheat Ridge, and West Third Avenue near Living Parkway

Emergency dispatch traffic referenced two separate reported assaults. One occurred at a Motel 6, and the other near West Third Avenue and Living Parkway. Medical personnel were instructed to stage nearby.

1:24 AM | Road Closure for Light Pole Removal

Table Mesa Drive and South Broadway, Boulder

Crews were removing a light pole, resulting in a roadway closure and a westbound bus detour. Passengers were advised they might need to exit at nearby stops and walk.

1:18 AM | Screaming and Breaking Glass Reported

West Kentucky Avenue, Denver

Officers responded after a caller reported hearing screaming, someone shouting “grandma help,” banging and glass being thrown at a residence. Additional units were dispatched.

1:00 AM | Police Check Hotel Room

Kipling Street, Lakewood

Officers responded after hotel staff reported possible unregistered guests. Dispatch indicated the registered guest might have an outstanding Edgewater warrant with a $500 bond.

12:46 AM | Disabled Bus

South Tower Road and East Louisiana Avenue, Aurora

Transportation dispatch received a report of a disabled bus. Units from the East Metro area were responding, and additional coverage was requested.

12:20 AM | Intoxicated Guests Arguing

Garrison Street, Lakewood

Police responded to an apartment disturbance involving several reportedly intoxicated adult men who refused to leave. The incident was described as no longer physical, with no weapons reported.

12:16 AM | Rollover Crash With Possible Injuries

E-470 near Peoria Meadows

Emergency crews coordinated traffic control and shoulder access following a reported rollover crash. Responders discussed moving the roadway closure point closer to a pedestrian bridge.

THURSDAY NIGHT | NOVEMBER 12

11:50 PM | Serious Injury Crash

Southbound I-25 at C-470

Emergency personnel responded to a reported serious injury collision. Traffic control assistance was requested while units worked at the scene.

11:50 PM | Late-Night Argument

Van Gordon Way, Westminster

Police were dispatched to a verbal dispute reportedly continuing since late evening, possibly connected to a party.

11:46 PM | Repeated Apartment Noise Complaint

West 14th Avenue, Lakewood

Officers responded after a caller made multiple complaints about loud noise at an apartment. Dispatch discussed providing responding officers with a building access code.

11:45 PM | Open 911 Call

West Mansfield Parkway, Lakewood

Police responded after a 911 caller reportedly yelled “Get out” before disconnecting. Callback attempts were unsuccessful. Dispatch noted previous calls at the location involving unwanted individuals.

11:41 PM | Motorcycle Collision and Fire

Northbound I-25 near E-470

A possible motorcycle-on-motorcycle collision was reported, with one motorcycle on fire. Traffic was reportedly shut down while crews diverted vehicles away from the ramp.

11:28 PM | Vehicle Strikes Mountain Lion

Lee Hill Drive, Boulder

A Ford Bronco or Jeep Wrangler reportedly struck a mountain lion. The vehicle appeared drivable, and no human injuries or traffic blockage were reported.

The mountain lion reportedly limped away from the area.

11:10 PM | Collision on Highway 285

Southbound US-285 near mile marker 247, Morrison

Dispatch reported a possible vehicle collision, with Indian Hills Fire responding.

11:04 PM | Domestic Dispute Involving Woman and Baby

West Sixth Avenue, Denver

Police responded to a reported domestic disturbance involving a woman carrying a baby. The woman reportedly left the area with the child while a man returned to an apartment.

11:02 PM | Domestic Fight at Quality Inn

11907 West Sixth Avenue near Simms Street, Golden

A domestic dispute was reported at a Quality Inn. A vehicle window was reportedly smashed, and a woman with a newborn was seen running toward Simms Street.

This may be connected to the separate West Sixth Avenue domestic dispatch two minutes later.

10:54 PM | Possible Overdose

West Colfax Avenue near Glendale Drive and Smith Drive

Fire and medical crews responded to a reported possible overdose or poisoning.

10:43 PM | Possible Impaired Driver at Red Rocks

Red Rocks Park and Amphitheatre, Morrison

A sedan was reported leaving the area with loud music and failing to slow down. The driver was subsequently reported returning and appearing impaired.

10:38 PM | Laceration Injury at 7-Eleven

West Colfax Avenue and Harlan Street, Lakewood

Engine 11 and Medic 11 were dispatched to a reported laceration injury at a 7-Eleven. Additional details were not available.

10:33 PM | Gunshots Reported at Short-Term Rental

Golden Eagle Circle, Golden

Deputies responded after approximately three gunshots were reported near a short-term rental property.

Officers made contact and interviewed a man. A person described over dispatch was reportedly seen walking along a fence line toward Highway 285. No confirmed arrest was included in the summary.

10:33 PM | Alcohol-Related Medical Emergency

North Boulder

Emergency crews responded to an 18-year-old woman reportedly intoxicated and vomiting near Boulder North. Her condition was not established.

10:30 PM | Disturbance on Crowded Bus

East 40th Avenue and Airport Boulevard, Aurora

Transit officers coordinated with a bus operator regarding a passenger reportedly vaping and behaving rudely. The bus was full, and the operator wanted to continue the route. An officer was requested to meet the bus and speak with the passenger.

10:10 PM | Person Reportedly Carrying Gun

East 62nd Avenue, Denver

Police received a report of a person carrying a firearm near East 62nd Avenue. No additional circumstances were confirmed.

10:05 PM | Unauthorized T-Shirt Vendors at Red Rocks

Red Rocks Park and Amphitheatre, Morrison

Staff reported unauthorized vendors entering through the north gate and selling shirts near the east stairs and east gate.

Rangers and police were requested, and staff were advised not to engage with the vendors.

10:02 PM | Possible Assault at Apartment Complex

North Chester Street, Aurora

Emergency medical personnel were dispatched to a possible assault at an apartment complex. Unit 14 acknowledged the call and responded.

9:40 PM | Suspicious Person Reported

South Sheridan Boulevard, Lakewood

Police were sent to investigate a suspicious person near a business. Dispatch also described the reporting party’s vehicle as a 2009 Chevrolet Silverado.

9:37 PM | Eight-Vehicle Crash Reported

Westbound I-70 near Sheridan Boulevard

Dispatch traffic described a possible eight-vehicle crash near Sheridan Boulevard. Multiple units responded, and a drone was reportedly used during a search for a driver. The roadway was subsequently reopened.

The available dispatch summaries also describe a multi-vehicle crash on Highway 6 near Sheridan. These should not be assumed to be the same incident without confirmation.

9:33 PM | Multi-Vehicle Crash Blocks Highway 6

Westbound Highway 6 near Sheridan Boulevard

As many as eight vehicles were reportedly involved in a collision blocking all three westbound lanes. Rescue crews responded, and officials discussed whether the location fell under Denver or Lakewood jurisdiction.

9:32 PM | Driver Leaves Crash Scene

Highway 119 and Jay Road, Boulder County

Officers responded to a two-vehicle property damage crash. One driver reportedly left the scene and may have lived nearby.

9:31 PM | Crash on I-225

Southbound I-225 near 17th Avenue

A possible split-scene crash was reported, with one portion of the incident affecting the left lane and another on the right shoulder.

9:25 PM | Stolen Hyundai Linked to Juveniles

West Virginia Avenue near Belmont Apartments, Denver

Police responded after a witness reported approximately eight juveniles driving erratically in two vehicles.

A Hyundai was reported disabled, while a dark hatchback left the area. Later dispatch information linked one vehicle to a newly stolen 2019 Hyundai Tucson.

9:25 PM | Road Rage on I-76 Ramp

Westbound I-76 ramp to Wadsworth Boulevard

A white Chevrolet Equinox was reportedly swerving and repeatedly braking in front of another driver. A license plate was provided to dispatch.

9:23 PM | Six-Vehicle Crash and Rollover

Westbound Highway 6 near Sheridan Boulevard

Dispatch described a collision involving approximately six vehicles and a separate rollover, with reference to an earlier terminated police pursuit. Felony eluding was the only charge mentioned in the available summary.

This appears to be an earlier report associated with the larger Highway 6 incident reported at 9:33 PM.

9:19 PM | Possible Shooting at Sporting Goods Store

East 36th Avenue, Denver

Police dispatch received a report of a possible shooting at a Big 5 Sporting Goods location. The available dispatch summary did not establish whether shots were fired or whether anyone was injured.

⸻

Reporting note: These accounts are based on publicly available emergency dispatch audio and automated dispatch summaries. Some incidents remain preliminary, and details may change as agencies release additional information. Reports of crimes, injuries, suspects and road closures should not be treated as independently confirmed unless specifically indicated.

text:
Trump the Fox, Cornered by the Hounds of the Blue Tsunami
AMERICA WEEK EPISODE 88  (VIDEO IN ITALIAN, TEXT IN ENGLISH)
By Stefano Vaccara
NEW YORK (ITALPRESS) – This week in America feels like something straight out of a movie. A Chinese spy, a billionaire brought down by sex scandals, Wall Street trembling, a Defense Secretary under fire, and a president who can feel the walls closing in around the White House.
Let's start with the spectacular downfall of #JensenHuang, the founder of #Nvidia, the microchip giant powering artificial intelligence. A company that reached a valuation of $5.7 trillion, becoming one of the driving forces of both the American and global economies.
#Huang resigned following revelations of two extramarital affairs. One with Alice Huang, a businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for China. The other with an executive at Nvidia itself. The company's stock plunged, sending shock waves through Wall Street and the entire technology sector.
Nvidia, after all, controls roughly 90 percent of the market for advanced AI chips. According to The New York Times, Trump had been warned by U.S. intelligence agencies and even by Secretary of State Marco Rubio about suspicions surrounding the alleged Chinese spy, yet he took no action. Meanwhile, Huang continued visiting the White House and influencing American policy on technology exports to Beijing. Now Congress wants to know what the president knew and why he failed to act.
Another potential investigation added to the growing list awaiting the Trump administration. Because the blue tsunami unleashed by the midterm elections continues to send shock waves across America.
The latest, a historic one, comes from Mississippi, where #ScottColom defeated Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, becoming the first Black senator elected from that state since Reconstruction, more than 150 years ago.
Mississippi, the land of segregation and the long struggle for voting rights, is sending a Black Democratic senator to Washington.
A victory that reveals just how profoundly America is changing, and Trump knows it.
In January, Democrats will take control of Congress, armed with investigative committees, subpoena powers, and the ability to compel sworn testimony. Investigations that could reach directly into the president's affairs, his family, and his entire inner circle.
Meanwhile, Pete Hegseth, the head of the Pentagon, has managed to freeze impeachment proceedings against him, at least for now. A reprieve that may last only until the new Congress takes office.
Even at Arlington National Cemetery, a military guard had to shout at the Secretary of "War" and his laughing entourage, ordering them to show respect and remain silent in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The video went viral.
Above all, there are still the Epstein files, with mounting pressure to reveal everything the Justice Department has yet to make public.
Trump is reacting the way he always has: by attacking.
In words, he offers cooperation to Democrats. In practice, he promotes Stephen Miller, the architect of his mass deportation policies, to White House chief of staff and orders Vice President JD Vance to investigate alleged corruption in Democratic-run states.
Corruption, of all things!
It looks almost like a preemptive reflex: accuse your opponents of the very wrongdoing you fear they may soon investigate you for.
Rather than a lame duck, Trump increasingly resembles a hunted fox. He senses his pursuers closing in and bares his teeth, convinced he can still frighten them away.
Yet this is precisely where he may be making his biggest mistake: the new Democrats arriving in Congress are not the same politicians who spent years seeking compromises with Trumpism.
Take Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's newly elected senator. He has made his position unmistakably clear: deference doesn't work with a bully. You have to confront him with even greater force, because a bully backs down when he discovers that someone is no longer afraid of him.
Then there's Bernie Sanders, an independent senator who is already leading a revolt against Chuck Schumer, the symbol of an old Democratic leadership accused of making too many concessions to Trump.
The battle to replace the party's leadership has begun, as a new generation of Democrats wants to move from resistance to the offensive.
Of course, Trump is also desperately searching for political breathing room, pushing for an agreement on Ukraine or Iran. But at this point, even a diplomatic breakthrough seems unlikely to stop the accountability process that the incoming Congress has already pledged to pursue.
Some argue that Democrats should focus more closely on the mandate voters gave them, concentrating exclusively on the cost of living and leaving investigations behind.
It's a false choice, especially since concern over rampant corruption in Washington was among the top priorities of voters who backed the Democrats.
American voters have come to understand that when corruption shapes government decisions, ordinary people's standard of living pays the price as well.
Trump may no longer be able to intimidate Democrats, but how much power will he have left when he discovers that his threats no longer work?
Trump built his power on other people's fear.
Starting in January, he will have to learn to live with his own.

🚨 Pakistan’s Mining Sector | NRL Identifies Copper-Gold Mineralisation Across 8 Discoveries in Chagai

National Resources Limited (NRL), a privately owned Pakistani mineral exploration company, has identified copper and gold mineralisation across at least eight porphyry discoveries in Balochistan’s Chagai district, following nearly 25,000 metres of drilling.

One drill hole returned an impressive 295-metre continuous mineralised interval grading 0.43% copper and 0.13 g/t gold, including a 132-metre section grading 0.83% copper.

The discoveries cover 5.6 square kilometres in Darigwan, adjoining NRL’s earlier Tang Kaur copper-gold discovery. The company is now progressing towards its maiden mineral resource estimate, subject to further exploration and international reporting requirements.

NRL is a joint venture involving Fatima Fertilizer, Liberty Mills and Lucky Cement. Chairman Muhammad Ali Tabba also reaffirmed the company’s $100 million commitment to mineral exploration in Pakistan.

The next phase includes environmental, hydrogeological, metallurgical and geotechnical studies in 2027, with a bankable feasibility study targeted by the end of the decade.

Key takeaway: The discoveries strengthen the potential of Pakistan’s mineral sector, although commercial viability, resource estimates and eventual development remain subject to further studies.

text:
A scientific demolition of climate-change denial

How a collection of genuine geological facts is manipulated to produce a profoundly misleading conclusion.

The passage is an unusually sophisticated example of climate-change misinformation. Unlike crude assertions that global warming is a hoax, it deploys genuine scientific findings, impressive geological timescales and apparently authoritative statistics. Much of its descriptive material is broadly correct.

But its central argument is scientifically indefensible. It confuses the conditions under which life evolved over hundreds of millions of years with the conditions under which human civilisation developed over a few thousand. It confuses the oceans' enormous capacity to absorb heat with an ability to make excess heat disappear. And it invokes natural processes operating over tens of thousands or millions of years to explain away a dramatic change occurring within a single human lifetime.

Above all, it commits one enormous intellectual fraud: because the Earth has been much warmer in the distant past, it concludes that rapid warming today cannot be dangerous.

That is about as sensible as arguing that because human beings can survive temperatures of 40°C, a sudden rise in someone's body temperature from 37°C to 40°C is nothing to worry about.

1. The 542-million-year deception

The author cites Judd and colleagues' important 2024 Science paper reconstructing global temperatures over the Phanerozoic Eon.

The research is genuine. Its use here is misleading.

Earth has indeed experienced much warmer climates, sometimes without permanent polar ice sheets. But these climates existed under radically different conditions of continental geography, ocean circulation, atmospheric composition and biological evolution.

Modern civilisation, agriculture, cities, infrastructure and coastal settlements developed during the comparatively stable climate of the Holocene, beginning approximately 11,700 years ago.

The relevant question is not whether dinosaurs inhabited a warmer planet. It is whether eight billion people, their agricultural systems, water supplies and coastal cities can accommodate extraordinarily rapid climatic change without immense disruption.

Furthermore, the geological evidence is not a refutation of carbon dioxide's warming influence. It helps demonstrate that influence: atmospheric CO₂ has been an important contributor to the great temperature changes in Earth's history.

2. The claim that 1,000 ppm of CO₂ would be 'ideal'

This is an assertion masquerading as science.

Carbon dioxide is essential to photosynthesis. Nobody disputes that. But the fact that a substance is necessary for life does not mean that increasing its concentration indefinitely is beneficial.

Water is essential to life too. That does not make flooding desirable.

The author offers no scientifically defensible basis for declaring 1,000 parts per million an ideal atmospheric concentration.

Pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ was approximately 280 ppm. It has now risen above 420 ppm, an increase of more than 50%, principally because of human activities.

The increase has been extraordinarily rapid by geological standards.

The scientific issue is not whether CO₂ is poisonous at current concentrations. It is whether adding it to the atmosphere changes Earth's energy balance.

It does. That is elementary, experimentally established atmospheric physics.

CO₂ absorbs and emits infrared radiation. Increasing its concentration reduces the rate at which heat escapes to space until the climate warms sufficiently to restore the energy balance.

The suggestion that because CO₂ was higher millions of years ago it cannot cause dangerous warming today turns the geological evidence on its head.

3. The oceans: the most revealing distortion

Here the author presents some largely correct information and then draws precisely the wrong conclusion.

Yes, the oceans store vastly more heat than the atmosphere.

Yes, they absorb approximately 90% of the excess heat accumulating in the climate system.

But consider what that means.

The oceans are absorbing the overwhelming majority of the additional heat trapped by greenhouse gases. They are not disproving global warming. They are recording it.

Ocean heat content has risen dramatically, and measurements show continuing accumulation of energy.

The oceans' enormous heat capacity delays atmospheric warming, but it does not prevent it. Nor does the energy simply disappear.

Warming oceans expand, contributing to rising sea levels. They intensify marine heatwaves, damage coral ecosystems and influence atmospheric weather patterns.

The author describes the oceans as the Earth's air conditioners. That analogy is deeply misleading. An air conditioner transfers heat out of a room. The oceans largely store and redistribute heat within the Earth system.

The distinction is fundamental.

4. Water vapour: the familiar greenhouse-gas trick

The author correctly observes that water vapour makes a larger contribution to Earth's natural greenhouse effect than CO₂.

But this is not an argument against human-caused warming.

Water vapour acts predominantly as a feedback, whereas the human addition of long-lived CO₂ is an important forcing.

As CO₂ warms the atmosphere, warmer air can contain more water vapour. That additional water vapour amplifies the original warming.

In other words, the very importance of water vapour makes CO₂-driven warming more consequential, not less.

The passage also confuses the relative contributions of different greenhouse gases to the existing greenhouse effect with their roles in causing the present increase in temperature.

These are two different questions.

5. Milankovitch cycles cannot explain the present warming

The author invokes changes in Earth's orbit and axial orientation.

These are real and important. Milankovitch cycles help explain the pacing of glacial and interglacial periods.

But their principal cycles operate over approximately 23,000, 41,000 and 100,000 years.

They cannot account for the extraordinary warming observed since industrialisation, especially during the last half-century.

Nor can tectonic movements, which generally operate over millions of years.

The passage effectively argues that because very slow natural processes can change the climate, a much faster human-induced process cannot do so.

There is no logical or scientific connection between those propositions.

The existence of natural causes does not exclude additional human causes.

6. 'We are still in an ice age'

Technically, yes.

In geological terminology, Earth remains within an icehouse state because substantial permanent ice sheets survive, particularly in Antarctica and Greenland.

But the author exploits a specialised definition to create a false impression.

Being in a long geological ice age does not mean that rapid warming within an interglacial is harmless.

Indeed, the great continental ice sheets are among the reasons global warming presents a long-term threat.

Their melting contributes to sea-level rise, potentially continuing for centuries or millennia.

The survival of polar ice is not evidence that additional warming is desirable.

7. The most demonstrably false claim: nobody would notice rising seas

The assertion that warming would raise sea levels by only a few millimetres, imperceptibly over a lifetime, is contradicted by direct observation.

Global mean sea level has risen by roughly 20–25 centimetres since 1900, with the rate increasing in recent decades.

That rise is measured using tide gauges and satellites.

It is already affecting coastal communities through more frequent tidal flooding, erosion and saltwater intrusion.

A few millimetres of additional sea level each year may sound trivial. Accumulated over decades, it is anything but.

And sea-level rise is not simply a matter of thermal expansion. Melting land-based glaciers and ice sheets also add water to the oceans.

The author has mistaken the small annual increment for the cumulative effect, and ignored the acceleration.

8. 'There is no global warming crisis'

This is not a scientific conclusion supported by the preceding evidence. It is a political declaration.

It does not follow from anything established about ancient temperatures, tectonic plates, ocean currents or orbital cycles.

Nor does it follow that wind turbines and solar panels are a 'terrible dead end'.

Renewable-energy technologies have environmental costs, including mining, land use, waste and ecological impacts. These deserve serious scrutiny.

But the relevant comparison is with the environmental and climatic consequences of continuing to burn fossil fuels, not with an imaginary energy system that has no adverse effects.

The author never undertakes that comparison.

The result is not a scientific argument but a polemic dressed in the language of science.

9. The most damning evidence is the paper the author cites

There is a particularly revealing irony in the reference to Judd et al. (2024).

The paper is entitled A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature. Notice, incidentally, that the actual reconstruction covers 485 million years, not the entire 542-million-year Phanerozoic invoked in the passage.

Its authors found a strong relationship between atmospheric carbon dioxide and global temperatures, identifying CO₂ as a dominant control on long-term climate variations.

That is virtually the opposite of what this polemic invites readers to believe.

Squarespace+1

The same reversal occurs with the oceans. The author cites their absorption of more than 90% of excess heat as though this makes global warming insignificant. In reality, measurements of increasing ocean heat content are among the strongest independent confirmations that the planet is accumulating energy.

Global Sea Level Change

And the sea-level claim is especially indefensible. The European Environment Agency reports approximately 23 centimetres of global sea-level rise since 1900, while NASA's satellite measurements show that the rise is continuing.

European Environment Agency (EEA)+1

10. What climate science actually says

There is an important distinction between the claim that warming is human-caused and the suggestion that uncontrollable, unlimited 'runaway warming' is inevitable.

The latter is not the mainstream scientific position. Climate scientists do not generally predict a Venus-like runaway greenhouse effect on Earth.

They do establish that human activities have unequivocally caused global warming, that additional greenhouse-gas emissions will produce further warming, and that the risks increase with its magnitude and rate.

IPCC

Recognising this distinction strengthens the scientific argument rather than weakening it.

A concise rebuttal suitable for publication

This is a masterclass in how to misrepresent science without necessarily inventing the facts.

Yes, Earth was warmer millions of years ago. Yes, CO₂ is essential to life. Yes, oceans regulate climate, water vapour is a powerful greenhouse gas, and orbital cycles influence ice ages.

But NONE of these facts refutes human-caused global warming.

Indeed, the 2024 Science paper cited by the author identifies atmospheric CO₂ as a dominant influence on Earth's climate over geological time. The oceans' absorption of 90% of excess heat is evidence of warming, not evidence against it. Water vapour amplifies CO₂-driven warming. Milankovitch cycles operate over tens of thousands of years, not decades.

And the claim that rising seas are imperceptible is demonstrably false: global sea level has risen approximately 23 centimetres since 1900, and the rate is accelerating.

The fundamental deception is to confuse the fact that Earth has survived radically different climates with the proposition that human civilisation can safely endure rapid climatic disruption.

Dinosaurs survived on a warmer planet. That tells us remarkably little about the vulnerability of modern agriculture, freshwater supplies, coastal cities or eight billion human beings.

This is not a refutation of climate science. It is a collection of scientific facts arranged to conceal the conclusions that follow from them.

The most revealing feature is that the author's own principal scientific source contradicts the argument being made.

Principal scientific references

Judd et al., Science (2024): 485 million years of Earth's temperatures

IPCC Sixth Assessment: Observed warming and its causes

IPCC: Greenhouse gases, water vapour and climate feedbacks

European Environment Agency: Measured sea-level rise

NASA: Ocean heat accumulation
The strongest way to challenge the original author is to ask one question: Why cite a major scientific paper about 485 million years of climate history while omitting its central finding that CO₂ is a dominant control on global temperature?
That omission goes to the heart of the argument.

text:

How a collection of genuine geological facts is manipulated to produce a profoundly misleading conclusion.

The passage is an unusually sophisticated example of climate-change misinformation. Unlike crude assertions that global warming is a hoax, it deploys genuine scientific findings, impressive geological timescales and apparently authoritative statistics. Much of its descriptive material is broadly correct.

But its central argument is scientifically indefensible. It confuses the conditions under which life evolved over hundreds of millions of years with the conditions under which human civilisation developed over a few thousand. It confuses the oceans' enormous capacity to absorb heat with an ability to make excess heat disappear. And it invokes natural processes operating over tens of thousands or millions of years to explain away a dramatic change occurring within a single human lifetime.

Above all, it commits one enormous intellectual fraud: because the Earth has been much warmer in the distant past, it concludes that rapid warming today cannot be dangerous.

That is about as sensible as arguing that because human beings can survive temperatures of 40°C, a sudden rise in someone's body temperature from 37°C to 40°C is nothing to worry about.

1. The 542-million-year deception

The author cites Judd and colleagues' important 2024 Science paper reconstructing global temperatures over the Phanerozoic Eon.

The research is genuine. Its use here is misleading.

Modern civilisation, agriculture, cities, infrastructure and coastal settlements developed during the comparatively stable climate of the Holocene, beginning approximately 11,700 years ago.

The relevant question is not whether dinosaurs inhabited a warmer planet. It is whether eight billion people, their agricultural systems, water supplies and coastal cities can accommodate extraordinarily rapid climatic change without immense disruption.

Furthermore, the geological evidence is not a refutation of carbon dioxide's warming influence. It helps demonstrate that influence: atmospheric CO₂ has been an important contributor to the great temperature changes in Earth's history.

2. The claim that 1,000 ppm of CO₂ would be 'ideal'

This is an assertion masquerading as science.

Carbon dioxide is essential to photosynthesis. Nobody disputes that. But the fact that a substance is necessary for life does not mean that increasing its concentration indefinitely is beneficial.

Water is essential to life too. That does not make flooding desirable.

The author offers no scientifically defensible basis for declaring 1,000 parts per million an ideal atmospheric concentration.

Pre-industrial atmospheric CO₂ was approximately 280 ppm. It has now risen above 420 ppm, an increase of more than 50%, principally because of human activities.

The increase has been extraordinarily rapid by geological standards.

The scientific issue is not whether CO₂ is poisonous at current concentrations. It is whether adding it to the atmosphere changes Earth's energy balance.

It does. That is elementary, experimentally established atmospheric physics.

CO₂ absorbs and emits infrared radiation. Increasing its concentration reduces the rate at which heat escapes to space until the climate warms sufficiently to restore the energy balance.

The suggestion that because CO₂ was higher millions of years ago it cannot cause dangerous warming today turns the geological evidence on its head.

3. The oceans: the most revealing distortion

Here the author presents some largely correct information and then draws precisely the wrong conclusion.

Yes, the oceans store vastly more heat than the atmosphere.

Yes, they absorb approximately 90% of the excess heat accumulating in the climate system.

But consider what that means.

The oceans are absorbing the overwhelming majority of the additional heat trapped by greenhouse gases. They are not disproving global warming. They are recording it.

Ocean heat content has risen dramatically, and measurements show continuing accumulation of energy.

The oceans' enormous heat capacity delays atmospheric warming, but it does not prevent it. Nor does the energy simply disappear.

Warming oceans expand, contributing to rising sea levels. They intensify marine heatwaves, damage coral ecosystems and influence atmospheric weather patterns.

The author describes the oceans as the Earth's air conditioners. That analogy is deeply misleading. An air conditioner transfers heat out of a room. The oceans largely store and redistribute heat within the Earth system.

The distinction is fundamental.

4. Water vapour: the familiar greenhouse-gas trick

The author correctly observes that water vapour makes a larger contribution to Earth's natural greenhouse effect than CO₂.

But this is not an argument against human-caused warming.

Water vapour acts predominantly as a feedback, whereas the human addition of long-lived CO₂ is an important forcing.

As CO₂ warms the atmosphere, warmer air can contain more water vapour. That additional water vapour amplifies the original warming.

In other words, the very importance of water vapour makes CO₂-driven warming more consequential, not less.

The passage also confuses the relative contributions of different greenhouse gases to the existing greenhouse effect with their roles in causing the present increase in temperature.

These are two different questions.

5. Milankovitch cycles cannot explain the present warming

The author invokes changes in Earth's orbit and axial orientation.

These are real and important. Milankovitch cycles help explain the pacing of glacial and interglacial periods.

But their principal cycles operate over approximately 23,000, 41,000 and 100,000 years.

They cannot account for the extraordinary warming observed since industrialisation, especially during the last half-century.

Technically, yes.

In geological terminology, Earth remains within an icehouse state because substantial permanent ice sheets survive, particularly in Antarctica and Greenland.

Being in a long geological ice age does not mean that rapid warming within an interglacial is harmless.

Their melting contributes to sea-level rise, potentially continuing for centuries or millennia.

The survival of polar ice is not evidence that additional warming is desirable.

That rise is measured using tide gauges and satellites.

A few millimetres of additional sea level each year may sound trivial. Accumulated over decades, it is anything but.

And the sea-level claim is especially indefensible. The European Environment Agency reports approximately 23 centimetres of global sea-level rise since 1900, while NASA's satellite measurements show that the rise is continuing.

European Environment Agency (EEA)+1

10. What climate science actually says

There is an important distinction between the claim that warming is human-caused and the suggestion that uncontrollable, unlimited 'runaway warming' is inevitable.

The latter is not the mainstream scientific position. Climate scientists do not generally predict a Venus-like runaway greenhouse effect on Earth.

They do establish that human activities have unequivocally caused global warming, that additional greenhouse-gas emissions will produce further warming, and that the risks increase with its magnitude and rate.

IPCC

Recognising this distinction strengthens the scientific argument rather than weakening it.

A concise rebuttal suitable for publication

This is a masterclass in how to misrepresent science without necessarily inventing the facts.

Yes, Earth was warmer millions of years ago. Yes, CO₂ is essential to life. Yes, oceans regulate climate, water vapour is a powerful greenhouse gas, and orbital cycles influence ice ages.

But NONE of these facts refutes human-caused global warming.

Indeed, the 2024 Science paper cited by the author identifies atmospheric CO₂ as a dominant influence on Earth's climate over geological time. The oceans' absorption of 90% of excess heat is evidence of warming, not evidence against it. Water vapour amplifies CO₂-driven warming. Milankovitch cycles operate over tens of thousands of years, not decades.

And the claim that rising seas are imperceptible is demonstrably false: global sea level has risen approximately 23 centimetres since 1900, and the rate is accelerating.

The fundamental deception is to confuse the fact that Earth has survived radically different climates with the proposition that human civilisation can safely endure rapid climatic disruption.

Dinosaurs survived on a warmer planet. That tells us remarkably little about the vulnerability of modern agriculture, freshwater supplies, coastal cities or eight billion human beings.

This is not a refutation of climate science. It is a collection of scientific facts arranged to conceal the conclusions that follow from them.

The most revealing feature is that the author's own principal scientific source contradicts the argument being made.

Principal scientific references

Judd et al., Science (2024): 485 million years of Earth's temperatures

IPCC Sixth Assessment: Observed warming and its causes

IPCC: Greenhouse gases, water vapour and climate feedbacks

European Environment Agency: Measured sea-level rise

NASA: Ocean heat accumulation
The strongest way to challenge the original author is to ask one question: Why cite a major scientific paper about 485 million years of climate history while omitting its central finding that CO₂ is a dominant control on global temperature?
That omission goes to the heart of the argument.

Peace talks to end the war in Ukraine could take a major turn as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy demands European nations directly join the negotiating team.

Here is the detailed, easy-to-understand breakdown of Zelenskyy's strategic gamble and the continued intense fighting on the ground:

1. "Europe is no bystander" (Zelenskyy’s big demand)

What happened: On November 13, at the European Political Community (EPC) summit in Dublin, Ireland, President Zelenskyy held high-stakes talks with U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.

He made a critical demand: "In the next round of peace talks, Europe must join as an active member of the negotiating team, not just as observers or mediators."

His reasoning: The war is being fought on European soil, so European security is directly on the line. Bringing Europe into the negotiation room gives Ukraine crucial backing, helping to ensure they aren't pressured into a bad deal or forced to give up territory without major security guarantees.

2. "Will Putin agree to European involvement?" (The U.S. envoy's take and Russia's view)

The U.S. Envoys' View: Following the meetings, U.S. Envoy Kushner shared a notable insight: when he asked Russian President Vladimir Putin if he would be open to "attempting" to include Europe in the negotiations, Putin seemed to show some agreement or willingness to consider it.

The Kremlin's Caution: However, the Kremlin has yet to formally confirm any acceptance. In fact, Putin threw skepticism at the U.S. envoys, saying, "The U.S. needs to figure out whether Europe actually wants peace for Ukraine, or if they are just looking to extend this war for their own interests." This highlights Putin's deep mistrust toward European nations that verbally call for peace while supplying weapons.

3. "Massive prisoner swap on the table, but evacuation routes contested"

A glimmer of hope: On a positive note, Zelenskyy expressed strong hope for an upcoming prisoner swap agreed upon during talks in Abu Dhabi, predicting it would be the "largest of its kind to date."

Disagreements over evacs: However, the two sides remain deeply split over Putin's proposal to evacuate trapped civilians from areas like Kostiantynivka in Donetsk.

Zelenskyy has stayed quiet on the offer, with experts warning that Putin might be using "humanitarian" routes as a PR stunt to demonstrate full Russian military control over these hotly contested territories.

4. Grim reality on the ground: "1,200 drones intercepted and civilian casualties"

While leaders debate peace, the battlefields remain brutal.

The Russian Ministry of Defense claimed it intercepted a staggering 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, in one of the largest coordinated drone assaults of the war.

The attacks reportedly hit oil and industrial facilities in southern Russian regions like Volgograd, killing four civilians. In retaliation, Russian forces launched heavy strikes on coastal areas near Ukraine's port city of Odesa, underscoring that a peaceful resolution remains far off on the ground.

To sum it all up!While Zelenskyy’s push to bring European nations directly into the negotiation room has been met with skepticism from Putin—who questions Europe's motives—peace efforts like a massive prisoner swap are being completely overshadowed by relentless warfare, including a massive 1,200-drone offensive, highlighting the immense gap between diplomatic talks and the brutal reality on the ground.
